PRIVATE MEMBERS' NOTICES OF MOTIONS- PRECEDENCE ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: I rise to a question of privilege affecting the members of the House of Commons. I refer you, Mr. Speaker, to page 13 of the routine proceedings and orders of the day, where you will find a resolution standing in my name under No. 10. It was my understanding before the house prorogued at the last session that resolutions for the new session could not be received or placed on the order paper while the house was then in session, and so the resolution standing in my name was sent in after the house prorogued; and it was dated September 3. Now I understand the resolutions which reached the office earlier than mine, and while the house was still in session, are on the order paper ahead of mine. I submit that if there is no rule regarding resolutions there should certainly be a definite rule as to the time resolutions can be put on. A resolution sent in while the house is sitting should be for that session, and a resolution sent in immediately after the house prorogues is intended for the forthcoming session. I am asking you, sir, to have the matter investigated, because I believe I have been gypped.

Atomic Energy

subtopic: REPORTED INFORMATION LEAK FROM CANADA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REPORTED INFORMATION LEAK FROM CANADA
speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. Press reports from Washington suggest that- Mr. Bernard Baruch, in evidence before a United States senate committee, indicated that a leak of secret information in connection with atomic energy had occurred in Canada. Is the minister in a position to give the house positive assurance that this has not occurred, and if not, will he cause an immediate investigation to be launched?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
subtopic: REPORTED INFORMATION LEAK FROM CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I read the press reports with surprise. It had been our view that all possible security measures had been taken in connection with our Canadian operations, and we had heard nothing to suggest that our friends in the United States had any other view. The question then arose as to whether Mr. Baruch was being quoted accurately, and I am happy to say it now becomes evident that he was not quoted accurately. I have just received a personal wire from Mr. Bernard Baruch. I may say that I had not communicated with him, but he took the trouble to communicate with me. His wire has been telephoned to me-I have not the original at this moment- and it reads as follows:
In view of the confused reports I feel impelled to tell you that there was nothing in my statement before closed session of the senate committee on atomic energy that in any way reflected on Canada or the present operations there. I did refer to the past spy activities of the Soviets in Canada which were as regrettable to you as they were to us.
Then follows a personal message to myself. I believe the Secretary of State for External Affairs can also throw some light on the wording of the statement as actually made by Mr. Baruch.
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): Mr. Speaker, when my colleague (Mr. Howe) and I were shown this newspaper report yesterday we both expressed concern as to the accuracy of the report, and I immediately endeavoured to ascertain just what the situation was. Just a few minutes ago I got from our ambassador in Washington the following report:
Concerning Mr. Baruch's reference to leaks in Canada, I have just succeeded in securing this morning the language actually used by Mr. Baruch, taken from the transcript. The only reference made by him to Canada during the public session of the committee was in the following sentence:
"As you can see by the newspapers this morning, Canada, one of the countries associated with us, has made some discoveries in plutonium and, which concerns me deeply, it was from Canada that the much publicized reporte of an information leak have come."
That was all that was said in the public session. It is a reference not to leaks coming from Canada but to the publicized reports that leaks had come from Canada. Then the report also points out that Mr. Baruch spoke in a very low voice and those in the committee room had great difficulty in following him. That may have been the cause of the distorted version of his remarks sent out yesterday. The chairman of the joint committee, Senator Hickenlooper, has told a Canadian correspondent that Mr. Baruch said nothing derogatory to Canada, Mr. Baruch's reference came in the middle of a fairly long discussion on the risks of information leakage, and later the committee went into closed session for a further discussion of means to maintain security. Now we have this assertion of Mr. Baruch that in the closed session nothing derogatory to Canada was said; and of course there was no occasion for anything derogatory to Canada being said.

subtopic: PRICE AND COMMODITY CONTROL-WARTIME ORDERS IN COUNCIL

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: PRICE AND COMMODITY CONTROL-WARTIME ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister, of which I sent him notice this morning? I understood it was the intention of the government to place on the Votes and Proceedings and on the order paper this week measures necessary to continue the policy of price and commodity control after the expiry of the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, as well as such measures as may be required for a considerable period to give statutory form to the orders in council enacted under wartime powers. I note that nothing has so far appeared in the Votes and Proceedings, and I suggest to the government that if these measures are to be presented next week, hon. members should be given the earliest opportunity of preparing to discuss them.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRICE AND COMMODITY CONTROL-WARTIME ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend is quite right in saying that the government had undertaken to place on the Votes and Proceedings the names of measures that were to be introduced for the purpose, as he said, of continuing the policy of price and commodity control under the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, as well as such measures as may be required for a considerable period to give statutory form to orders in council enacted under wartime powers. I had myself expected to see these measures enumerated in the Votes and Proceedings today, but I understand there was a delay in the forwarding of the measures. The Clerk of the House has just advised me that he has now received the list which will appear in the Votes and Proceedings of today and on the order paper the day following. But I might give the house immediately the information that I think hon. members will be most anxious to have.
The legislation which will be submitted to parliament in respect of emergency powers will be divided into two categories:
1. The government will introduce about fifteen bills which, if adopted, will replace by legislation a number of orders in council which it is considered should in the national interest be placed on a more permanent footing. All of these relate to subjects which are within the normal competence of the parliament of Canada.
This legislation will include bills to amend the Fertilizers Act, the Inspection and Sales Act, the Feeding Stuffs Act, the Customs Act,

the Militia Pension Act, the Militia Act, the Patents Act, the Department of National Defence Act, the Canadian Grain Act, the Wheat Board Act and the Immigration Act (as regards return to Canada of Canadian Chinese), and bills respecting mail contract supplements, trading with the enemy, export and import controls and agricultural products.
2. The government will introduce a bill to provide for the continuation for a limited period of certain transitional measures to the number of about fifty.
The regulations covered by this bill will constitute all of the emergency powers of the government at this stage of transition from war to peace. It will provide for the extension of a group of orders, including those respecting control of prices, supplies and rentals, together with regulations for the return to Canada of remaining dependents of service personnel, settlement of claims against the crown arising out of the war, administration of Japanese property in Canada, relocation of persons of Japanese race, old age pensions and certain compensations to merchant seamen. All of these will be specified in a schedule to the bill. I have a tentative list here, but I think they can be given later.
A certain number of the orders which will be specified in the schedule will be the subject of additional specific bills later in the session. This would apply, for example, in the case of labour relations, which will be covered in a bill to amend the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, orders regarding old age pensions which will be covered in a later bill to amend the Old Age Pensions Act and orders regarding veterans' preference in the civil service, which will remain in the schedule pending examination of this subject by a parliamentary committee with a view to later introduction of legislation.
Apart from the measures which will be covered by the legislation I have referred to, all other orders in council under the emergency powers will either have been revoked, expired or become spent or will be permitted to expire with the expiry of the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, 1945.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO VETERANS BEING PERMITTED TO COMPLETE MATRICULATION REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
I
should like to direct a question to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, of which I gave him notice. Groups of veterans are still being required to cram the work of five years into six months, and are in fear of losing all their educational gratuities. Would the minister care to make a further statement on the matter?
Right Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Veterans Affairs): I may say at once that there has been a misconception in regard to this whole question. Many of these matriculation students up to now have finished their courses in a lesser period than six months; of course some have gone through the usual period of eight months and some have gone twelve months. This scheme is carried out with the cooperation of the Minister of Labour and with the active cooperation-and it has been very good-of the department of education of the province of Ontario. From both
Inquiries of the Ministry

these sources we have the assurance that the necessary facilities will be provided for training as long as they are required for those who are making reasonable progress. There is no change whatsoever in the policy; those who within six months have shown marked promise will be encouraged to take their examinations, for the reason that the universities have changed their policy in reference to having a special session to which the veterans have been invited early in the year, because if they missed the present October term they might have to wait for several months, which is not so good for their education, before again having an opportunity to enter university. In regard to facilities, in regard to encouragement, in regard to providing every amenity for the continuation of their studies, there is no change whatsoever in policy; and we have the splendid cooperation of the Department of Labour and, as I said, of the department of education of the province of Ontario.

Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): Mr. Speaker, the question is in very general terms: have there been any developments in that field? Members of this house I am sure have followed with interest the reports of the deliberations of that convention which have appeared in the press. However, we have received no communication in this connection from the Newfoundland authorities; and of course it is a matter for the Newfoundland national convention and the appropriate authorities in Newfoundland to decide whether an approach will be made to Canada regarding possible confederation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext:
The house resumed from Monday, February 3, consideration of the motion of Mr. J. W. MacNaught for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and
The Address-Mr. Brunelle
the amendment thereto of Mr. Bracken, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was not in the house when the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacNaught) and the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cournoyer) moved and seconded the adoption of an address in reply to the speech from the throne. However from what I read and from what I have heard it would seem that they did honour to their task; and upon that I congratulate them. Both are promising young men. I congratulate them even more because it is my intention to ask today for shorter speeches m house debates. Those two hon. members set a good example by delivering brief but most effective speeches when they moved and seconded the adoption of the address in reply.
At this stage of the session I believe it is in order to suggest some amendments to the rules of the house. However, such suggestions have been made so often, without results, that I entertain but little hope of success. In the words of Mark Twain, everyone talks about the rules of the house, but no one does anything about them. Governments come and go, but the house rules, some of which are obsolete and meet with neither the wishes nor the approval of hon. members, remain.
I suppose therefore that conditions will continue as before: during the first part of the session there will be very little done, and during the latter part of it we shall be in a great hurry, with the result that things will be half done.
In the first place it would seem that all parties should agree to limit to twenty minutes instead of forty the time permitted for speeches. In the second place it would seem that the debates on the address in reply and the budget, and speeches offering amendments, should be limited to the speeches of the leaders of the parties in the house or their substitutes. It would make very little difference whether the debate on the address in reply lasted one week or two, or one month or two months, because the final vote is taken on the address submitted in the first instance, with no change.
It is true that those votes amount to votes of confidence in the government. I submit however they cannot be classified even as proper occasions for votes of confidence, because there are points in the speech from the throne and in the budget which all hon. memb*-s approve, and there are others of 
which some hon. members disapprove. Yet we have to vote either for or against the whole thing.
I believe further that at the opening of each day's sitting hon. members in opposition groups should be somewhat less inquisitive and ask fewer questions. It will be recalled that only this afternoon we lost more than half an hour from the asking of such questions. If hon. members wishing information were to write the different departments from which they require that information, they would receive replies in writing. Further, the political platforms of the respective parties in the house are now well known to all. Debates would be improved if they were shortened, if we heard a little less about purchasing power, directive economy and negative criticism, and more of really constructive suggestions.
After all, I believe all hon. members wish to preserve the well-being of our citizens. If we look back twenty-five years we must conclude that today we are doing very well. Conditions in general are as good as they could be. Living conditions in European countries do not compare with those in Canada; our only point of comparison is the United States, and anyone who has been in that country since the end of the war has found out that life and business in Canada are greatly to be preferred. Over here there is work for everyone, with the exception of a few unfortunate cases. Wages are good, and the epidemic of strikes which followed the conclusion of the war has almost disappeared. This is due to the good work of the department, and not to accident. In justice at this point I would pay a compliment to our Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell). During the war his task was no less delicate than it was difficult, and he fulfilled it masterfully. No one has worked harder, and for his ability, for his competence, for his judgment, yes. for his endurance, he deserves the thanks and felicia-tions of every Canadian. The Minister of Labour is a labour man. He is an honest unionist; he did a great deal for his fellow *men before he came to this house, and in this house he has done honour to the high post of Minister of Labour. It has been a pity to hear the bitter criticisms and the unfair attacks which have been made against him by some of the labour leaders and by some hon. members in this house who pretend to be specially concerned with labour. But in spite of ail this, the name of our Minister of Labour will go down in history as being that of one of the best we have ever had.
We hear a great deal of talk about the adoption of a labour code. Of course this will provoke opposition and indignation on the

The Address-Mr. Brunelle
part of certain knights errant who are always in quest of fights against windmills in the name of the autonomy of the provinces. As usual we shall have to adopt a course which will help the labouring class. If a labour code is desired by the labour unions, and if it will help to bring the level of wages paid to the workers in the province of Quebec up to the level of the wages paid to workers in other provinces, I will be in favour of it. We must satisfy the labouring class by just and practical means. We must give it happiness and contentment in order to save its members from falling into the ranks of the extremists. Industrial activity should be encouraged in every way in order to create jobs and accentuate production in general.
Having that in mind I wish officially to ask the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) to do his utmost to sell or to rent or to give away the building or the war plant known as Electric Steels at Cap de la Madeleine. That plant should not be allowed to deteriorate to the extent that the building will become useless. Later on I shall privately give the minister my reasons for making this request in such an urgent manner. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) visited the plant recently with me, and was greatly impressed by its size and value. I intend to use him as a witness when I plead my case before the Minister of Reconstruction.
I should like to refer to another class of worker who deserves the particular solicitude of the government-the agricultural worker. Industrial workers have their unions to protect their members, but the farmers have no union. I doubt if they will ever have a really efficacious union. I speak for the farmers of all Canada. I am opposed to special privileges and special financial favours being granted to one portion of agriculture. The eastern farmer as a rule does not spend much time asking for favours. In fact he has never been spoiled by government favours. The same thing cannot be said of the farmers in other parts of Canada. If there is any difference between the eastern and western farmer I would say that the eastern farmer works harder and longer hours and is a more deserving citizen. He is honest and he pays his debts. He administers his affairs more wisely and more economically than others. He takes good care of his property. You will not see near the buildings of an eastern farmer pieces of expensive machinery like threshing machines, combines, binders and mowers lying around exposed the year round to rust and dust and rain and snow. Fortunately the eastern provincial government have not passed any moratoriums
or shielding laws, if I may call them that; they have not passed any protecting laws that actually invite the farmer to be dishonest.
Be that as it may, the tillers of the soil are entitled to the special attention of any government. Even if a farmers' national union could be formed, it would not be as effective as the unions of other workers. The reason for that is self-evident. The farmer must work twelve hours and more a day; he must work on Sundays; he must work on legal holidays. He cannot charge or be properly remunerated for overtime work. The cattle, horses, sheep and hogs on his farm will not allow the farmer to take a holiday during the summer. In general the farmer receives no more than seventy-five per cent of the remuneration received by other workers. His task is far from being easy or light; it is far from being pleasant. Yet how essential is the production of the farmer!
I should like to give some statistics. I submit that the present prices of butter and eggs are not sufficiently high, and I shall limit myself to discussing those two items. In reality $2.50 per hundred pounds for liquid milk, or raw milk as they call it, is no more than a fair minimum price. It may be that such a price is paid in certain places, but it certainly is not general. On that basis, a net return to the farmer of 60 cents per pound for butter should be made possible either by new or additional subsidies or by the application of the provisions of the Agricultural Prices Support Act which was passed in 1944. In proportion a price of 60 cents per pound for butter would be less than what we pay for other consumer goods like shoes, clothing or canned goods.
In justice I must say that the present government and the present able Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) have been good to the farmers. But the actual conditions call for more protection for the farmer. I profess to be fairly well acquainted with farming conditions in the east as well as in the west. I have many friends on farms in my constituency of Champlain, and I have farms in the province of Saskatchewan from which I draw a great deal more worry' than money. In general the income from the farm does not compare with the income received by other manual workers, either in terms of dollars or in terms of energy spent. In brief, subsidies or bonuses ought to be provided to raise the price at least of dairy products to the farmer. In some places, Mr. Speaker, farm labour is asking far more in daily wages than the farmers are making themselves. The
The Address-Mr. Brunelle

serfs are getting more than, the kings of the earth. The great writer, Lamartine was right when he wrote:
The plough in making the first furrow laid the foundation of society. It is not only wheat that grows out of ploughed land; it is civilization itself.
I intended to speak of rationing and controls, but I shall have to refrain in order to practice that brevity of speech which I preached at the outset of my remarks. I shall only say that the sooner we recover our full liberty, the better it will be for all concerned. Perish that bureaucracy which now afflicts Canada. If the sacrifice of something which is dear to us must be made, well and good; but we must remember that all of us in every sphere of activity are always jealous of our liberty, and I think that the country mouse in the fable expressed the current feeling:
Give me again my hollow tree,
My crust of bread and liberty.
According to an investigation made recently by the Department of Reconstruction, building materials will be available in almost sufficient quantities in 1947. In order to prepare the way, I suggest that a time limit be now set for the expiration of controls and that the greatest possible publicity be given to that time limit. In the meantime all interested parties would prepare to face the situation which sooner or later must be faced. I do not think there will be much of a shortage problem at the expity of that time limit, except in some special cases, like Ottawa, for instance, where shortages prevail more than anywhere else-except a shortage in speech-making-and where possibly the municipality could assume the responsibility with the generous aid of the government or perhaps with the aid of some provincial premiers such as the premier of Ontario and the premier of Quebec, who with their autonomy complex might be willing to take over. They actually did take over the milk question a short time ago, and the price of milk thereafter went up by' three to four cents a quart. But just the same, long live autonomy-!
There are certain small grievances of which vre are all anxious to rid the country, but in justice it must be said that Canada is still the best place in the world in which to live. And for that fact the present government deserves some credit. The members of this house are all no doubt determined not only to maintain our present advantageous condition but to improve it. Canada is stoutly heading towards her great destiny. The obstacles, if any, will not come from bey-ond our borders but from ourselves. If there is discord among our Deople, if there is suspicion

and distrust among us, or in a larger field if there is no cooperation between the governments of the provinces and the central government, our advance will be slower, and our progress might be brought to a standstill.
Yesterday I listened with interest to the long lecture given by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) and to his remarks on the progress of the federal-provincial negotiations. I notice that he made many suggestions. I think, Mr. Speaker, he could help a great deal if he would only speak to his provincial Tory friends in Ontario and Quebec and ask them to cooperate more in fact than in words. It is a known fact that the premiers of Ontario and Quebec are playing politics with this question. Every Tory in the countiy knows it and enjoys it, and every Liberal and every good Canadian knows it and deplores it. If the leader of the opposition does not know it, I would not like to pass judgment on the merits or demerits of his innocence. However that may be, already we have achieved much. Canada has attained the status of a prosperous free nation, ranking third in international trade, making her own treaties, signing her own commercial pacts, exporting huge quantities of goods, having ambassadors in every nation. In brief, Canada in the eyes of the world is a land of unlimited promise. We are all without exception proud of these achievements, because we all want a greater, a happier and a freer Canada-freer in practice, freer in fact, and even freer in appearance.
As a last word I would say this. In the face of the refusal of the big four, Britain included, to make Canada a party to the peace treaties, in the face of that painful disillusionment, it seems more than ever expedient for every Canadian, for every member of this house to stand united and to proclaim his self-reliance, his independence, yes, his self-respect, and to agree to adopt as a first move a neat and tangible sign, a distinctive flag which will symbolize to all the world, our Canada, our home, our native land.
Mr. DONALD M. FLEMING (Eglinton) (Translation): Mr. Speaker, before commencing my speech in English I should like to refer to the loss which this country and this chamber have sustained since the last session in the death of Hon. P. J. A. Cardin. Warm tribute was paid last Friday by the leaders of all parties in this house to his memory and to his services to this nation. Need I say, Mr. Speaker, that I associate myself with this well deserved tribute.
I had not known Mr. Cardin before I became a member of parliament one and a half years ago. I am happy to say that, not-

The Address-Mr. Fleming
withstanding the difference in our ages, the acquaintance which we then formed grew into a warm friendship, and I was indebted to him on many occasions for assistance, encouragement, counsel and his generous confidence. In his passing, which has so greatly impoverished this house, I personally mourn the loss of one of the greatest Canadians of his generation, an esteemed friend, a man of honour and principle.
(Text): It is to me a special pleasure, Mr. Speaker, to have this opportunity of saying a word of welcome to this chamber to two new members, the member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Miller) and the member for Parkdale (Mr. Timmins), both of whom happen to be my personal friends. I should like to say to you, sir, that I am confident they will contribute much to the dignity and the decorum of the chamber, as well as to its deliberations. The member for Portage la Prairie has done the nation a great service in bringing before the people the verdict of western Canada on those deplorable aspects of the wheat agreement entered into by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) with Great Britain. As regards the member for Parkdale, having sat with him in former years in the city council of Toronto I predict that he will add greatly to the knowledge of this chamber on the pressing problem of housing as well as on a number of other leading national problems.
1 cannot forbear a word of reference to certain events which have taken place since this parliament prorogued on August 31, 1946. I cannot fail to deplore and at the same time to condemn the attempt on the part of certain members of the government opposite in the Pontiac by-election to stir up racial and sometimes religious feeling. I was in that riding in that campaign and I know of my own knowledge some of the things that were done by hon. members opposite, some on the treasury benches, in stirring up racial and religious feeling. It is deplorable.
Many of us approach this session with special interest because we have long wished to know more and wished the country to know more about the exact relationship between the Liberal party and the C.C.F. party; and it is to be hoped that at this session we shall learn something concerning that relationship. Perhaps the amendment which has been introduced by my leader, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Blacken) will provide an opportunity for the clarification of these relationships.
I am not going to remind the house of those occasions in the two previous sessions on which the leader of the C.C.F. came to the rescue of the government when it was in difficulties. I am not going to delay the house by reminding it of a statement made by the leader of the C.C.F. last year concerning the approaches made to him on behalf of the Liberal party, asking him to lead the Liberal party, or a Liberal-C.C.F. coalition. Incidentally, we have never been told just who it was who made those approaches on behalf of the Liberal party; but we had some assurances last session from the Minister of Agriculture-I am glad to congratulate him as the Right Honourable the Minister of Agriculture -that it was not he who made them. The next step was what he no doubt considered the honourable proposals of marriage which were made by the Prime Minister in his Quebec speech of November 29. A-wooing he went, and he invited the C.C.F. to align themselves under his banner.
The first reaction to these matrimonial proposals apparently did not come from the leader of the C.C.F. in this house. The first record I have been able to find of any notice taken of these proposals of marriage by a responsible figure in the C.C.F. party shows that it was taken by provincial reconstruction minister J. H. Sturdy of the Saskatchewan government. Mr. Sturdy is quoted in a Canadian press dispatch of December 6 as follows:
It was generally known at Ottawa that Prime Minister Mackenzie King's choice as a successor to leadership of the Liberal party was C.C.F. national leader M. J. Coldwell.
Mr. King's "strategy for heading off a Tory government is some kind of union of the C.C.F. and the Liberals," Mr. Sturdy said.
"I would rather see the C.C.F. sink, if necessary, in a blaze of glory than sell out to any party with its roots in the dead past."
The member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) in due course got around to giving the official answer on behalf of the C.C.F. group, and it seems that the Prime Minister is to receive a negative answer to these proposals. That seems to be, as nearly as one can tell, the gist or substance of the speech made in this house last night by the member for Rosetown-Biggar, notwithstanding the cordial way in which he was received by the government benches when lie rose to speak.
I suggest that the amendment which my leader has introduced will afford the C.C.F. party an opportunity of saying to this house and, if they wish, to the people of Canada, whether they are or are not in fact an opposition party. We have seen many evidences
The Address-Mr. Fleming

of a working alliance between the government and the C.C.F. forces in this house. Here is an opportunity for the C.C.F. really to come out in the open and say what the relationship is between them. The amendment will give them their opportunity to say whether they have confidence in this government in the light of its record.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, it was a matter of great regret on the part of members of this house, regardless of their political affiliations, that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in his speech yesterday did not take advantage of the opportunity to supplement what was lacking in the speech from the throne-a lack which is perhaps its most conspicuous feature. He had the opportunity to give the house some information about the programme of the government, because in the speech from the throne there was certainly no information but rather a mass of vague and meaningless platitudes. If the government has a policy or a programme to bring before the house at this session, we know just as much about it now as we did when the Prime Minister rose to speak. If there is such a programme, we are still waiting to hear it.
I am sorry, sir, that the Prime Minister is not in the house at the moment, because I wish to make reference to some of the things he said last night, and also to the way he said them. I am sorry the Prime Minister saw fit to make some of the remarks he did last night, and I should like to refer particularly to one of them. He began his remarks, as hon. members will recall, by making some reference to the facial expressions of members in this part of the house. I should like to have said to him, had he been here, that his own facial expression presented an interesting study, especially when the amendment was introduced by the leader of the opposition. I should like to tell the Prime Minister that when he undertakes to refer to the position which my leader holds with reference to this party and the affections of us who stand behind him, the Prime Minister or any other leader in this house might very well envy the loyalty and the affection which the members of the Progressive Conservative party accord to the leader of the opposition. The Prime Minister need not waste any time or any tears in making comments about the position of the leader of the opposition with reference to this party. His position is secure and we look forward to his assumption at an early date of the reins of office on the treasury benches.
No member of the house coming to this 1947 session, Mr. Speaker, dare close his eyes to the condition of this country. Some reference has been made to the fact that employ-

ment is at a high level. Yes, as we all know, it is at a reasonably high level, in a general sense, although in many local areas unemployment is rife. But that condition of employment has been induced by loans abroad. Let us just take stock of the country at the present time. Agriculture and primary producers have been penalized by government policy. They have been footing the bill for government policy, as regards both price control and assistance to nations abroad. That load which should have been spread equitably over the whole population has been borne by the primary .producers, and in particular by the farmers. Labour in Canada today is restless and suspicious. It has lost all confidence in this government. It has not forgotten that the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board told the industrial relations committee of this house last summer that he just had to hold the increase in wages in the steel industry to only ten cents per hour, otherwise we would have inflation down on our shoulders. What happened? Within three months wage ceilings were removed entirely, and labour has lost all confidence in this government. Mr. Speaker, the white collar class is in a more difficult plight than I think the government has ever begun to realize. They have been squeezed between the upper and nether millstones: on the one hand, inflexible salary ceilings, with no escape clause at all; on the other hand, tremendous increases in taxation and rising costs of living. The provinces have been set at sixes and sevens by the policies of this government. Unhappily there are many evidences that the youth of the country are losing the confidence that all of us would wish youth to have in this land and its future. Thousands of the best-trained of our youth are seeking employment in the United States. As a parliament we cannot, we dare not stand still in the face of that situation. Our first duty as a parliament is to the youth of Canada, because with them lies the future of the country.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, there is that great northland, that land of treasure in which development work within the past year has received tremendous set-backs as a result of the blindness of this government. It is all very well for the government to make a gesture, to throw out sops to the mining industry in the form of slight decreases in taxation, but that does not get to the heart of the problem. The big producers are not the ones who need help. The ones who need help are those who are engaged in exploration and development work, those on whom the future hopes of this country for pros-

The Address-Mr. Fleming
perity depend to a greater extent than I think many in this chamber even yet realize. Over all is the picture of a country overburdened with an oppressive load of taxation, a load of which the people must be relieved in a measure before this session of parliament prorogues.
We had some interesting remarks from the Prime Minister last night on the subject of controls. It seems that once again the Prime Minister has donned the armour of the defender of the supremacy of parliament. Some of us would have liked to see him during these recent years carry the banner of the knight defender of the supremacy of parliament, but he chose to cast himself in a different role. Now he invites the plaudits of the house and the country because now in 1947 the government is proposing to put these controls on a statutory basis instead of an order in council basis. Well, if ever a man condemned himself and his administration it was the Prime Minister when he spoke on that theme in the house last night. If it is the policy of the defender of the supremacy of parliament that in 1947, if controls are to continue, they should be put on- a statutory basis, why did not the Prime Minister advocate that policy in 1946? Why did he not advocate it in 1945. instead of building up by means of order in council administration this gigantic bureaucracy which has assumed powers which should be exercised only by parliament?
Yes, I think the Prime Minister has forgotten much, and when he challenged the house last night to bring forward examples of how the government had done violence to the principle of the supremacy of parliament, I am afraid that while he was berating others about their short-sightedness, he himself was guilty of short memory. It is not so very long ago, Mr. Speaker,-you will remember the occasion very well, in September 1945-that an announcement was made in this house by the then minister of national health and welfare to the effect that two days before the government had set up the Canadian information service, and without so much as coming to parliament and without so much as saying by your leave, had transferred to the account of the Canadian information service appropriations voted by parliament in the previous session for the wartime information board. We tried to get some information about it, but were prevented from doing so; the government stood in our way and denied us the information. Yes; there is a good example of what order in council administration has meant under this government.
Not only that, Mr. Speaker. Has the Prime Minister forgotten the events of August last,
when for fear of a defeat in the house the government freed its own members in the debate on the subject of the milk subsidy, and the house voted by a substantial majority against any interference with the subsidy? But the government, headed by the same Prime Minister, went blithely forward and in a matter of a few days did away with the milk subsidy, in the face of the plain expression of opinion by parliament. Is that his conception of the supremacy of parliament?
And has the house forgotten that it is not more than two months since the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board went on the radio in a series of five broadcasts and laid down policy as far-reaching in its scope and effect as any declaration that has been made by any member of the government, including the Prime Minister himself, since the general election of May, 1945? Think of it! Great pronouncements of policy coming from a man who has no direct responsibility to this chamber! If our surprise was great on that occasion, how much greater was it when we were told by the same very able gentleman a few days later, that he had not consulted the minister to whom he is responsible, the Minister of Finance, and had not consulted the government before making that series of broadcasts. Could you want any better or more complete example of bureaucracy running wild? Could you want any better example of the flouting of the supremacy of parliament, any better proof of the fact that talk coming from the government today, doing lip service to the supremacy of parliament, is a pretty hollow exhibition.
Before I leave this theme, Mr. Speaker, may I say this by way of statement of the position of those of us who sit in this part of the house. We do not like bureaucracy. We do not like officials to enjoy vast powers without direct responsibility to this house. In our approach to this whole problem of controls, when we see this legislation I think it fair to say we will have two principles before us; first, the necessity of giving adequate protection to the consumer, and second, the necessity for stimulating production in this country, for without a great stimulation of production in Canada we will still be assailed with fears of inflation. The only way we have to cope adequately with the problem of inflation in this country is by increasing production tremendously, so that scarcity may be replaced by plenty.
The C.C.F. party is still on the same
course. They are still saying to us, in their amendment, that they want controls; they want controls made permanent in this country; they want to go on shackling the enterprise of
The Address-Mr. Fleming

the people of Canada. They want regimentation, because they believe in it, because they know very well that you cannot have a socialistic state without the regimentation of the people in that state. They may talk as they like about not believing in totalitarianism, but they are preaching a system which contains the inevitable seeds of totalitarianism.
Then may I say this word on the subject of taxation. If the government does not bring before this house at this session proposals for a reduction in taxation, before they have finished with this session they will know that they have had a fight on their hands with the Progressive Conservative party. We are here, Mr. Speaker, to fight for reductions in personal taxes in this country, and make no mistake about it. While the government have been silent on this question hitherto, we hope we may know soon what their plans are. They were not so careful before the 1946 session. You will remember that one minister of the crown, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann), undertook before the session opened to promise great reductions in taxation. Perhaps the government has grown wiser since then, but in any event there has been no intimation from the government as to whether or not they propose to bring about a reduction in taxation at this session. We of the Progressive Conservative party intend to fight for reductions in taxation at this session. We believe that high taxation is contributing very greatly at the. present time to the threats of inflation, because high taxation is increasing labour costs and the cost of materials, and is contributing very greatly to increases in prices.
I turn now, Mr. Speaker, for a moment to the housing scandal in this country. I am sure I do not need to recall to this house two events of importance in connection with this matter which occurred during the 1046 session. The first occurred on March 20 and March 22 of last year, when the Prime Minister and the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply in their speeches in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne painted such a glowing, bright picture of housing conditions in Canada. It was the same thing the Prime Minister said last night, about how much better conditions are here than anywhere else in the wide world, without any reference at all to the opportunities we have in this country for coping with housing conditions. On that occasion the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply painted a very bright picture of the outlook for improved housing. He went on to say in an expansive way, "Why, lumber probably the least of

our worries in Canada in the field of housing materials." Well, it was rather a chastened Minister of Reconstruction who came before this chamber on July 22 of last year and made the abject confession that not only was the housing situation in Canada worse than it had ever been admitted to be by the government in times past, but that by March 31, 1047, the situation would be twenty per cent worse than it was on March 31, 1046. Even that admission was made on the assumption that this country would build 60,000 housing units in the year 1946.
Well, we shall be waiting with interest for some final statement on the housing units completed in Canada in 1946, but the fact remains that at least one prophecy which the government made on that occasion has been abundantly fulfilled; that is, that housing conditions in Canada today are worse than they were last year. It is a deplorable fact; and the responsibility for that deplorable condition rests on the doorstep of this government. After all the lavish promises with which they sought the confidence of the people of this country during the election campaign in 1945, what a fulfilment is this! And when the people of this country have the opportunity they will bring home to those responsible for thus deluding them the responsibility for this housing scandal in Canada today.
Did it not amuse this chamber last evening to hear the Prime Minister praise the government for the number of building permits being issued in Canada this year? He took great satisfaction from the issuance of building permits, and pointed to the fact that if these building permits this year were all translated into houses the programme would be expanded to vast proportions. I cannot take time to refer to all he said last evening, but he stated that the building permits ran to $382,000,000 in 1946 and these are just preliminary returns to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics from 204 municipalities. That is one of the things inherently wrong at the present time, one of the things which have bulked large in the government's mismanagement of this housing problem. The fact of the matter is that they have not taken the plain course any government with its eyes open ought to have taken, to put curbs on building construction that was not contributing directly to the production of houses. You would think the Prime Minister considered it a virtue to issue building permits in this country for a lot of structures that could very well wait until the housing needs of the country have been met.

The Address-Mr. Fleming
In that connection it is not necessary to take any words of mine; I would quote the words of Brigadier Storms, who is the general manager of Housing Enterprises of Canada Limited, a company, as you know, made up ninety per cent of public capital and ten per cent of private capital contributed by lending institutions in this country. This is what Brigadier Storms had to say on October 9, 1946, both on the subject of the need in Canada today and the way in which building materials and labour are being permitted by the government to be diverted to construction other than the construction of houses. I quote from the Toronto Globe and Mail of October 10:
Bricks, cement, plumbing, electrical fixtures and other materials which should be going into housing are being used for millions of dollars' worth of non-essential building, Douglas H. Storms, general manager of Housing Enterprises of Canada Limited, asserted yesterday in an interview.
"This country has gone berserk on building of the wrong kind," he said. "Everywhere you see plant extensions, theatres, garages, stores, summer cottages, dance halls and hot-dog stands under construction. You can't tell me those buildings don't take material away from housing because they do. What is more, they are absorbing thousands of workingmen who should be building houses.
"At the same time, people are living in the worst distress for lack of houses. On one street of small houses in New Toronto, we found that each house was occupied on the average by 19 people. All this non-essential building goes on and we cannot get houses built for homeless people."
And he continued further:
"The public should be made to realize how awful this situation is," he said. "Thousands of people, many of them veterans back from overseas, are doubling up with their in-laws and in some cases living four and five in a room."
Then he goes on to speak about the dangers, and he says:
I am telling you that if those people cannot get warm places to live in this winter, there will be riots.
That is strong language, Mr. Speaker, but you know what the danger is. Then he continued:
"If you can show me a municipality in Ontario which is exercising the slightest selective control over building I'll buy you a new hat," Mr. Storms exclaimed.
During the war and the ensuing control period building was restricted, he said. Once the restrictions came off business corporations and individuals, all with money to spend, had rushed in to build. Firms were now building big plant extensions which, he said, would stand empty a few years hence "when the honeymoon is over."
It is regrettable that the government has taken no steps to put an end to this honeymoon in the construction of non-essential buildings.
I now turn to another subject, that vexed one of dominion-provincial relations. I represent a constituency in Ontario, but in approaching the problem of dominion-provincial relations I wish to make it abundantly clear that I do so not merely as a. resi-. dent of that province but as a Canadian. It is a problem national in scope, one which holds the interest of Canadians in all parts of Canada, or should.
We of the Progressive Conservative party say, first, that a way must be provided for the dominion and the provinces to reach agreement. Secondly, if an agreement is to be effective, it must be nationwide. We would not take away from any of the provinces which have signed an agreement any benefits they may have obtained. But we do say that this matter of reaching agreements cannot be fully effective in the solution of national problems unless such agreements are extended from coast to coast. We say further that that necessary nationwide agreement cannot be achieved without a general dominion-provincial conference.
The provinces-all of them-are ready to sit down together in conference. They have asked for a resumption of the conference, and the responsibility for failure to resume rests with this government. It is their refusal that prevents the reconvening of the conference today.
As did my leader last night, on this subject I speak more in sorrow than in anger. The method the government has pursued is wrong. In the first place, the idea of starting out with certain inducements and trying to gather in all the provinces on the basis of those inducements; then, when it is found such inducements are not enough, raising the ante so as to gather in more, and when it is found that that is not successful, raising the ante even more, cannot be acceptable; that method of horse-trading is inherently wrong. It is wrong in principle.
We recall the very proper terms of condemnation of such methods expressed by the premier of New Brunswick on January 6 of this year when he described as an affront the method pursued by the dominion, namely that of raising the ante after signing the agreement with him. He said it was creating gross discrimination, and of course he was entirely right. It is very easy for the dominion to raise the ante because the taxpayers have to pay it. But that is not a proper method.
The Address-Mr. Fleming

In the second place, the method of secret negotiation is not a proper one. This procedure of making terms or negotiating agreements with one province without disclosing to that province the terms of agreements negotiated with other provinces is likewise wrong in principle. These negotiations should be brought out into the open where the people of Canada can see them. Otherwise we shall have created an .intolerable situation which inevitably will lead to jealousy and distrust.
In the third place, nothing could be more un-Canadian or inimical to the spirit of confederation; yes, to the very fabric of confederation itself, than this tactic of playing off one province against another, or trying to create fissures in our national unity. Had that been the spirit prevailing in 1864 and subsequently we know there would have been no confederation. The fathers of confederation met together for a common purpose in an attitude of give and take. It was not a situation wherein one party was resolved to lay down in a high-handed fashion certain proposals and to refuse to meet in conference with the other parties unless he had his own way on his own terms. There would have been no confederation on that basis. Today the provinces are willing to confer. Why does not the dominion government, in the name of reason and in the name of Canada, call them together?
It is regrettable also that the government has pursued the policy of writing agreements on only one particular aspect of a problem which it admits has three aspects. It is not enough to confine these agreements to the field of taxation. They must be extended to include the other two matters embraced in the original proposals of the dominion, namely public investment, which will have so great a bearing on employment in this country in years to come, and social security, for which the people of Canada are looking today.
The speech from the throne does intimate that the provinces are to be called together in general conference. We find this at page 3 of Hansard, where it is stated that they will be called for the purpose of seeking agreement in the two other fields. Just think of it I They are going to be called together to discuss the two fields of public investment and social security. Yet this dominion government persists in its refusal to call them together to discuss the three proposals, namely those two and the field of taxation as well.
So far as the government of Ontario is concerned, I am glad it has made clear that it does not begrudge the other provinces anything they may get, because the government of

Ontario has admitted the necessity for a readjustment of taxation powers in order to bring about fiscal equality as between provinces. I am glad Ontario has taken that attitude. The government of my province has been realistic, and properly so, in its insistence upon a proper definition of responsibility in the crucial days which lie ahead, as between the dominion and the provinces, and an understanding of what sources of revenue the provinces will have to meet their responsibilities.
The provinces must have the assurance that, having given up the principal fields of taxation which Ontario and Quebec have indicated they are prepared to rent to the dominion, the lesser fields of direct taxation will be left to the provinces so that they may retain their autonomy in days to come.
I urge on this house that because of the state of frustration in which so many people find themselves today as they survey the plight of housing, the plight of the taxpayer, the plight of labour and the white-collar worker and the plight of the primary producer, and as they look at the government suffering from a state of coma, surely the time has come when this house should measure up to its responsibilities and interpret the will of the people of Canada in this chamber. I submit that the proper interpretation of that will is to be found in the want of confidence amendment introduced by my leader, the leader of the opposition.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the interests of
brevity I am not going to waste time in complimenting the mover (Mr. MacNaught) and the seconder (Mr. Cournoyer) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) did that last night for this group. They did exactly what was required of them. They eulogized the government and said that everything the government had done during its tenure of office was absolutely correct. They did not disappoint anyone on that side of the house, nor did they disappoint anyone on this side. The chances are that I, too, will not disappoint anyone this afternoon.
When I listened last evening to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) answering the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) I sat here and wondered if I were living in the Canada the Prime Minister was talking about. The rosy picture of peace and prosperity which he painted is certainly not applicable to the part of Canada from which I come. This debate provides an opportunity for every hon. member to place himself on record as to

The Address-Mr. Gillis
whether the prosperity painted last evening by the Prime Minister is applicable to the people who sent him here. If he does not do that, he is remiss in his duty. As I say, it is certainly not applicable to the part of the country from which I come.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar the speech from the throne leaves much to be desired. It does mention that certain matters will be discussed, and in one section it states that labour relations will be discussed. That is not anything new in this house; what will be new is to have something done about the matter. I trust we shall be able to persuade the government to give more than lip-service at this session to this very important question.
During the last session of the house I rose in my place here and attempted to avoid a strike in the steel works in my part of the country which would affect some 4,500 members of my constituency. Because of faulty labour legislation, because the government had taken the attitude of sitting back and hoping for some miracle to happen, that strike developed and it affected a very important section of that community. It lasted for months and it has left scars there which it will take years to remove. A great disservice was done to that particular part of the country. I place the responsibility for that squarely upon the shoulders of the government because this situation was developing for months and in my opinion it could have been headed off.
I again find myself facing a condition where
13,000	coal miners in Nova Scotia are placed in a similar position. For months they have been endeavouring to come to some kind of reasonable understanding with the operator. At the time when the matter of a new contract arose this government had full responsibility in the field of fuel. But nothing was done. The controls were removed and the problem was handed back to the provincial government. A stoppage of work developed which lasted for forty-eight hours. The miners are now back for two weeks with a federal commissioner attempting to resolve the dispute.
I should like to ask why that federal commissioner was not injected into the picture earlier? It is much easier to iron out that kind of problem before a work stoppage occurs. What authority has that federal commissioner to make any award except to report to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) ? He has none. His function is merely to try to get both parties to come to an agreement. In my opinion there is no possibility of the operator in Nova Scotia and the mine workers
coming to an understanding without government assistance. If there was, it would have been done long ago because they have had months of negotiation.
With a federal commissioner in there at this time, where does it leave the Minister of Labour in connection with the statement he made a few days -ago in answering a question I had asked? I asked the minister if his department was making any progress in resolving this dispute and the minister brushed off my. question very lightly with the answer that it was merely a local problem. A problem that affects the basic industry of the province, around which the economy of the province is built, means more to me than just a local the federal government poured millions of dollars into it by way of subsidies and subventions? Why. have they done that if they problem. If it is a local problem why has accept no responsibility for some regulation of the industry? I think the minister will have to revise his thinking on that particular matter because brushing it off with an answer of that kind is not going to solve the problem.
The issues in this particular dispute are quite simple and in my opinion the miners are very reasonable in their demands. There are only two main points at issue. First, the workers were asking for an increase of $2.50 a day. If that increase is granted it will merely put them in line with the wage rates now paid in western Canada. It costs just as much to live and a man must work just as hard in the mines of Nova Scotia as does a man in the mines of western Canada. But the miners got nowhere with the coal company with that demand. The second main point at issue- there are others, but they are not so contentious-was the establishment of a welfare plan, something that is in vogue in most of the coal mining districts of the world.
Having got nowhere with the company in connection with these demands, the executive board of the union visited Ottawa a couple of weeks ago when they spent almost two weeks with the Minister of Labour and his deputies They, were not adamant about their first demand of an increase of $2.50 a day because they dropped that down to an increase of $1.40 a day. That showed that they were willing to cooperate by modifying their demands. That revised demand meant that they were still approximately $1 a day behind the miners in western Canada. There was nothing done in Ottawa. The minister proposed setting up a conciliation board.
The machinery that existed in 1907 and the machinery that we have today by way of conciliation is not adequate to handle the
The Address-Mr. Gillis

problems of the industrial worker in this country today. We need new machinery. The company in connection with the proposal they made attempted to lead the people to believe that they were offering an increase of SI a day in the wages paid the mine workers of Nova Scotia, but in reality they were offering nothing. The offer they made was that for every point of increase in the production of coal in Nova Scotia they would increase the wage rates ten cents. What are the possibilities of increasing production in the coal mines of Nova Scotia? To my mind they are verv poor, and for many reasons. First of all, the company proposes more mechanization. To a limited degree that may be possible. There may be in one or two collieries a section which might be more highly mechanized. But the company took the attitude when negotiating with the executive board of the union that any coal derived from the mechanized end of the collieries would not be pooled with the general output and would not be included as increased production. That was completely dishonest. It was something the miners could not accept as an honest gesture on the part of the company to increase wages..
Second, while there are as many men on the payroll in the mines in Nova Scotia today as there were in 1939, there are 500 fewer men actually loading the coal. That means that the man who is actually loading the coal today is producing just as much coal as he produced in 1939 and it is physically impossible for him to increase that output to a greatei extent than at present. He is carrying an additional load of 500 datal men at the end of that shovel.
Third, there were 5,000 enlistments from the coal mining area, approximately 3,000 of whom came back on the payroll of the mines after three to five years of war, suffering physical handicaps. They are not in a condition to go down into the mine and mine coal. Many of them are obliged to go back into hospital periodically for medical check-ups, and so forth. But all that is counted as absenteeism, and that is why the rate of absenteeism appears to be so high in these collieries. That is another factor which militates against increased production in these collieries.
Coupled with these factors is the fact that mining machinery to-day in the coal mines of Nova Scotia is badly run down, because during the war it was impossible to get the mining machinery required, the picks and drills and shovels and things of that kind, and it would take considerable time to re-equip the mines with the machinery that is required.

So in reality in tying up the increase in wages with the proposed increase in production the company in my opinion was completely dishonest. It was trying to fool the men because by reason of the factors I have mentioned there is no possibility of increased production in these particular collieries.

speechtext: The hon. member said that the increase was tied to ten cents. Ten cents per what?

speechtext:
Ten cents for each point by which production is increased. There are ten points to a ton. If you raise it ten points, you raise it a ton.
With respect to the welfare plan, that is a question which in my opinion was settled twenty-two years ago, when the Duncan commission, under Sir Andrew Rae Duncan, investigated the coal mining industry of Nova Scotia and made a thorough analysis of all the factors involved. Might I point out that every recommendation in the Duncan report that was in the interests of the company has been implemented, every last one of them. The only recommendation that would benefit the mine workers and their families, the establishment of a welfare plan, was ignored, and it has been ignored for over twenty-two years. The company at that time absolutely refused to have anything to do with a welfare plan for the benefit of the mine workers. The Duncan commission recommended in clear and plain language the establishment of a welfare fund and set out not only the way in which the fund should be established but the mechanics for administering it. The Duncan commission recommended:
This fund should be constituted by contributions from all the operators of coal mines, to the extent of one cent per ton of coal raised, and by contributions from the province from the royalties which they receive in respect of the ownership. of the mines, to the extent also of one cent per ton of coal raised. If these contributions wrere continued for a period of five years, a fund would be constituted which would go a long way to improve very materially the surroundings in which the miners live, and to afford the miners and their families reasonable opportunities for social, physical and intellectual development.
The report goes on to recommend how the fund should be administered. That recommendation has lain in the archives of the provincial government for twenty-two years, after a great deal of money had been spent in the preparation of the report. But as I

The Address-Mr. Gillis
said before, every last recommendation in the interests of the company has been implemented. The only recommendation that benefited the men has lain buried in the archives of the provincial government for twenty-two years.
There are perhaps no coal mines in the world that are more hazardous to work in than the coal -mines of Nova Scotia. The general public, who have no intimate knowledge of the life that a coal miner leads, think of him as a person who is immune to danger, a person without human feelings. My conception of the life of a coal miner is this. Every time he leaves his home to go down into the coal mine, he is in exactly the same position as a soldier going into the front line because that may be the last time he will ever see his home. His wife and family are human too, and if he does not come back they feel just as badly as the banker's wife and family would do under such circumstances. But the general conception of the public is: Oh, well, they are just miners; they are used to these things; they are immune to the ordinary human feelings in regard to danger and death.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that you cannot compute the wages of a coal miner on the basis of dollars and cents and I am safe in saying that any member of this house who ever had the experience of having to earn his living and support his family from his labours in a coal mine would take the same attitude, if he suffered the kinks in his spine and felt all the fears that necessarily attach to a coal miner's life.
I have a few statistics here of casualties in a coal mining industry, and they read more like war casualties. They are United States figures but they are applicable to Canada in proportion to population; indeed perhaps the rate of casualties in Canada would be higher.
I have the figures for every year from 1941 to 1945, but I shall not take time to put them all on the record. I will simply give the totals. In that five-year period, in the bituminous industry in the United States there were killed, 5.598; injured, 251,547. In the anthracite industry, during the same period, 1941 to 1945, there were killed, 963; injured, 71,326. The total for the two branches of the industry was 6,561 killed and 322,873 injured. The average number injured annually between 1930 and 1944 was 66,968. The number of permanently totally disabled and permanently oartly disabled from 1930 to 1944 was 1,004,524. If one examines the operation of the coal mining industry since it began he 83166-7
will see that its casualties approximate the casualties of war. Its casualties are a continuing thing, taking place year after year.
The men who go down into the bowels of the earth into a coal mine are in my opinion producing the most essential commodity in this country. They work harder and cripple themselves sooner than anybody else and you cannot haggle and quibble on the basis of dollars and cents when it comes to compensating such men. They shorten their lives by fifteen or twenty years doing their job and taking the risks they do, with only a small share of the recreation and the things that the average man enjoys. You cannot compute the compensation for that sort of occupation on the basis of dollars and cents. The house should know these things and, what is more, the men who are examining into the industry and making recommendations with respect to it should know something about the conditions.
That brings me to the royal commission's report. To me, the report was one of the most disappointing documents I ever read.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: This year's?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

This year's report. Hon. members will recall that year after year since coming into this house I have emphasized and urged the necessity for a thorough examination of the coal mining industry of Canada with particular reference to the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Finally the government got around to making that examination, and when the minister of munitions of that day spoke in the house in tabling the order in council which was to set up the commission, as indicated by Hansard of March 27, 1944, at page 1850, he said:
Therefore, the government will appoint a royal commission, charged with the duty of studying all aspects of the production and distribution of coal in Canada, to report to the government with recommendations for such alterations of the pre-war coal policy as its lindings may indicate as necessary or desirable.
That language would lead me to believe that the minister not only wanted to examine the industry for the purpose of finding out its disabilities, as to whether it was uneconomic and so forth, but intended the commission to recommend to the government the adoption of a national fuel policy whereby the mines of Canada could be expanded and markets made available and, I should think, the country zoned. The commission fell far short of that. In short, the royal commission on coal recommended absolutely nothing. They amassed a lot of evidence; but having gone over the problem year by year for the last thirty years,
I can tell the members of this house that there is nothing in that report in the way of evidence

The Address-Mr. Gillis

which is new to me or which should be new to the government, because if they will dig back in their archives they will find brief after brief, both from the east and from the west, setting out the problem exactly as it was stated to the royal commission.
But the disappointing part ofi the commission^ report is that they recommend absolutely nothing. As regards any recommendations that were made to the government either by the unions in their briefs or by others, cold water has been poured upon them and nothing done, and all that the commission recommends is a continuation of the pre-war subventions, the elimination of subsidies as quickly as possible, the abolition of production subsidies, the industry being made to stand upon its own feet.
What, does all that add up to? It simply means that the industry must go back to the thirties, with no more assistance than that. What was the situation in the coal mining industry of Nova Scotia in the thirties? It was this. Thousands upon thousands of boys who subsequently went to fight the war were walking the streets without an. opportunity to get a job, and; in the second place those who were employed in the industry were working, on the average, two and a half days a week, having to eke out an existence on a relief basis.
That is what the commission recommends the mining industry of Canada to go back to. In the development and mechanization of the industry they recommend that the overdue mechanization of the Nova Scotia mines should be effected by the operators without capital assistance from government funds.
I was a member of the reconstruction committee that sat in 1942. The members of the committee will remember that we had the heads of the operating company in Nova Scotia here, and on the question of developing the industry and mechanizing it they said it would take a large capital outlay which they were not prepared to make. They did not have the finances. Only recently one of the mines in Nova Scotia, No. 18 colliery, which is petering out, has come into prominence. There is a good seam that overlies No. 18 colliery, having millions of tons of coal. It employs 450 men at present but it will have to be closed down in six months' time. At a cost of $1,000,000 a tunnel could be drifted from the present site of operations, the facilities that are there being made use of, and we could have a mine that would last for years, a mine around which millions are invested in churches, schools, homes and so forth.
