subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
About six feet. While the federal government had control of the industry they made a start at drifting the tunnel. They were prepared to go ahead with it but as soon as the war ended and the controls came off they dropped it. For the last three or four months, as the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) will remember, representations have been made to him to do something about the matter, but the old alibi comes up-it is now a matter of provincial jurisdiction. And the provincial governments sit back and say, "We have no money", while the coal companies say, "We cannot make the expenditure". So another asset goes by the board because there is a shortage of money.
The royal commission says that is the correct attitude to take. Our own industry is not important. We are getting plenty of toal from the United States and it may be more profitable for some people in this country to import United States coal than to develop the coal mining industry of Canada a3 an asset for the Canadian people.
One thing the royal commission did not probe is the question, to what extent are the Dominion Steel and Coal in Nova Scotia importers of United States coal? I came up on the train with one of the top heads of that corporation in 1943, and I made the observation, "You have backed out of the Quebec market and the Ontario market as in the last war. What will you do to regain it when the war is over?" He said, "We are not worried about that. We have not lost a customer in Ontario and Quebec. We are importing sufficient coal from the United States to keep all our customers in Ontario and Quebec." Have they discovered they can get more money out of a scheme of that kind than they can in developing and expanding their own industry in Nova Scotia? Some time I should like some minister of the government, when he has a chance, to tell the house to what extent the operators of that industry are importing United States coal and retaining the customers they had in prewar days.
It looks to me as if the determined plan of the Nova Scotia mining industry is to shrink it to care for maritime needs only, get clear of paying subventions, get clear of paying subsidies, and leave it there as another forgotten factor in Nova Scotia. Then those who have exploited the industry as long as it was profitable and as long as they could milk the public treasury of Canada, will go into the importation of coal from the United States, because

The Address-Mr. Gillis
that is a lucrative business when one examines the drawbacks and so forth that they get on the coal which is imported into Canada.
Another thought that I should like to leave with the government is this. I am absolutely opposed to the judiciary being used on royal commissions that are probing industry and I am absolutely opposed to their heading up boards that are dealing with labour relations. I have all the respect in the world for them in their own field, in the field for which they were trained. What is the situation in Nova Scotia with regard to the judiciary? They are being used for every other purpose than the one for which they were appointed. This is the situation in Nova Scotia at the present time. We have seven judges of the supreme court and they have to look after circuit duties and from time to time constitute the court of appeal in the province. There is a good deal of work in that. One of the seven men, Judge Carroll, has been away for over two years. He was on the royal commission. During that time he may have attended to some of his duties, but I do not know that. Anyway, he was away for over two years. Judge Smiley has been dead for the past eighteen months and no successor to him has been appointed.

I was twenty-six years on the end of a pan shovel. If I were summing up the evidence that was before that royal commission. I would tell the Canadian people truthfully that there was only one agency in this country that was capable of rehabilitating the coal mining industry of Nova Scotia, and that was the federal government. The provincial government admit that they are not able to handle it. I am reasonably sure they would be willing to hand over the control of that industry. The capital expenditure necessary to rehabilitate it can be made by only one agency in. this country and that is the federal government. I want to say this: in my experience with that industry, the only time that there was any satisfaction whatsoever, when we got our wages adjusted in any kind of reasonable manner, had them stepped up and avoided strikes, was during the period when the federal government controlled the industry during this war. There were then the best relations that ever existed in the industry. As far as I am concerned, as long as I am in this house, and can honestly do it, I am going to fight for the mining industry of Canada to be taken over by the federal government, because it is the only agency in this country which will develop it. If we want to sit back
The Address-Mr. Gillis

and take the attitude that we are going to lean on the arm of the United States for our fuel requirements, if we are not going to develop these resources, then we have no right to lay claim to this North American continent. Do not make any mistake about it; if you are watching the press, you will come to the conclusion that if the federal government or some other agency in this country is not going to do something about the eastern end of Canada, the United States is likely to. The stocks of this very corporation that I am talking about have gone away up on the market. They are being bought in the United States. British capital invested in this industry, according to press reports, has passed to interests in the United States; and you are very likely to find in the very near future an industry', in both steel and coal, in that end of the country developed to take care of the overseas market, a situation which is likely to make some of my friends in Ontario and Quebec squirm. I am reasonably sure that if they can set themselves up and go into that overseas market, they will cut the central Canadian product out completely. I am not objecting. However, I am a Canadian and I want to see Canadians develop Canadian resources. Mind you, I am not arguing against someone going in there and doing something about something that we are not touching. But I do want to see us develop our own resources rather than have people from the outside come in and take over.
I should just like to say a few words with regard to one of the new members of the house. I do not want to be unkind to any new member, because I remember when I came here myself, and I was very grateful for the way in which I was received and the patience that most of the members had with me. There is a strike on at the present time in Noranda, Quebec. It has been on for some time. One of the major issues in that strike is recognition of the union and the revocable check-off, where a man signs a card signifying his willingness to have his union dues checked off. That strike has been going on for some months. It is likely to interrupt the whole mining industry of northern Ontario. I have seen a report that they are likely to lay their tools down. I noticed an article in the Ottawa Journal of January 30, 1947, and I mention this because it deals with the issue in that strike. I am going to read this clipping. The new member to whom I have reference is the Social Credit Union des Electeurs member for Pontiac (Mr. Caouette); I am afraid my French is not very good:

Real Caouette, social credit union des electeurs member for Pontiac, told the Journal on his arrival in Ottawa for the session to-day that his party is flatly against the check-off for labour union or for any other purpose.

In conclusion, may I say, Mr. Speaker, that the disabilities I enumerated with respect to my own end of the country are fairly general throughout Canada. The reason is very clear. We are trying to hang on to the old machine that dragged us through two wars. We are still blundering along without any philosophy in life; and as long as the dominant factor in this country is the making of money we shall have what we have today. What Canada must do and what every member of this house must do is place human values above the dollar sign and work for the alleviation of misery among mankind. Mr. GEORGES E. LAPALME (Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm): Mr. Speaker, if it is customary to wish newcomers to this house the most sincere welcome and the greatest success, it is quite natural for a member on this side to insist all the more on the great victory of the new member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cournoyer), my neighbour to the south and my confrere at the bar. May he find in this house the ties of friendship which bestow upon political life the only attractions it can offer.
I do not intend to deal at once with the proposals put forward in the speech from the throne. However, may I point out the new trend in the legislative measures concerning the future, and I also feel at ease in approving ihe proposals of the government with respect to amendments to the Old Age Pensions Act, the establishment of a committee to consider and report upon the question of human rights, and the measures to be taken to provide an increase in the membership of the house.
For the time being I am withholding my praise and my criticism, and I wish to dweil upon a subject which I believe affects parliamentary operations to a greater extent than the proposed legislation itself. I am referring to the mechanism of legislation, or rather to the mechanism of parliamentary operations or procedure. I was very much surprised a few moments ago to hear the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Brunelle) express exactly the same ideas as I had in mind in relation to parliamentary discussions and the length of our debates. However, I was glad to see him change his direction and leave it to me to discuss this matter at length.
At the beginning of this month, February, who could answer the following questions: How long will we stay here and, when we leave next summer, how much work will have been done? Most hon. members can make a guess at the length of the session and put it at six or seven months. No one, however, could predict within ten per cent the total of our achievements. The reason is that the time lost in this house cannot be figured out. Fifty per cent of the speeches, even if they are very well prepared, are useless and never change a single vote; and owing to the obsolete rules and regulations of this house a discussion can be unduly prolonged and stretched out. In the meantime, days and weeks go by, and the only results are speeches lost in Hansard which no one reads except members, a few newspaper men who have to read them, and a few constituents to whom copies of their member's speech may be sent.
During the last two sessions, while sitting in this house and listening to speech after speech, I have often wondered if the population of this country would not have gained more from parliamentary operations if we had fewer speeches and more positive votes. I am not referring to votes on technical points, with which I shall deal later on. I am referring to a vote which immediately puts into effect in the life of a nation an important measure which otherwise may be implemented only weeks later. It is the nation which loses these weeks, while speeches gain thereby. After the last session a few newspapers raised the following problem with which I wish to deal: Would it not be appropriate to redraft the rules and regulations of the house in order to speed up the passage of our legislation? I think only last week the same question was brought up again in a national magazine.
I have good authorities to support this suggestion. Last fall in New York, before the United Nations the head of the Canadian delegation, the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent), who was then Minister of Justice, denounced with good reason the length of the discussions, and requested that speeches be limited to a veiy short period of time. He spoke for only ten minutes. I wish I could be as brief, but since the legislator is above his own laws probably I shall take forty minutes to request twenty or thirty minute speeches. Should not a measure which was considered appropriate for the United Nations, the organization of the world, also be excellent for the administration of our country? If it can be held that certain delegates of the great powers speak for local consumption, cannot the same thing be held against members of the Canadian parliament?
The Address-Mr. Lapalme

Here is a resume of what has been written, in various newspapers and national magazines:
How many members would ever speak at all were it not for the radio, newspapers and Hansard, in other words for the spot-light which shows them off before a permanent audience? It is an open secret that publicity^ granted by newspapers and specially by columnists prompts many members to rise to their feet at every occasion. After three or four speeches, one is proud to read in newspapers that he is on the list of future cabinet ministers. Those who remain mum because they think too many talk -too much, stay in the background and are considered by their constituents as inert and incompetent back-benchers.
During two sessions, which is approximately nine months, I spoke only once. It is useless to add that since I do not run after publicity I was not overwhelmed by it. Many other lion, members did the same. A few have not even yet made their maiden speeches. What would have happened if all of us had decided to speak in every debate? We would still be here completing the work of the fall session of 1945.
It is very easy to see the ridiculous side of this situation, and it is easy to understand to what extent the positive operations of the house may be delayed, and are delayed, by the laxity of the rule. How can this situation be remedied? By carrying out the recommendation the Secretary of State for External Affairs suggested at a meeting of the United Nations, to the effect that they limit the length of speeches. This time limit should be set at twenty or thirty minutes, with the exception of party leaders; and one should be authorized to read his speech.
I am told that this suggestion has already been made in the house. I come with it again. Reading one's speech means that it has been prepared most carefully and that it will be on a higher level. It also means greater speed in delivering it, thus avoiding hesitation and repetition on the part of those who think they can improvise. Those who overstep their limit of forty minutes are usually those who do not read their speeches.
Furthermore, although all French-speaking members speak English, they would rather have a prepared text when they address themselves in that language. This is easy to understand. since some of their English-speaking colleagues, who have a natural command of the English language, never speak without staring continuously at their texts.
Therefore, what about those like myself who speak a tongue which is not their own. However, the imposing of time limits on speeches will not be sufficient to prevent what, to use a common expression, might be described as a parliamentary bottleneck. As a

matter of fact the present rules allow 244 members-not including yourself, Mr. Speaker -to speak for forty minutes on the debate in reply to the speech from the throne, and to say anything at all. When this marathon is over, we shall then vote. And we shall vote upon what? Upon legislative measures? Not at all. The speech from the throne is nothing more than the statement of a programme, and it is always carried by a subsequent vote. Then, why all these speeches-including my own' We should ration speeches. There should be no debate on the speech from the throne. Last year I believe the debate lasted for three weeks. Why should not participation in these debates be restricted to the official leaders of our political parties, or their representatives?
All this noise over the speech from the throne is nothing in comparison with the time lost oyer the voting of the estimates and the meetings of the committee set up for the purpose of studying bills in all their details. We listen to all these unnecessary debates leading to dull votes on technicalities, and speeches from eight to ten members, all approving the same measure, when it is not even opposed; and members' resolutions which are killed by speeches. I am omitting many more.
Sometimes the debate on the estimates looks like a marathon of endurance and boredom. Each member should be entitled to ask only one question on each item. This question could be subdivided into a few more. Once the answer has been given by the minister the member could discuss or accept the answer in a speech which should not last for more than ten minutes.
The detailed study of bills in committee usually lingers over an unjustified period of time, owing to the great number of speeches delivered which often wander away from the subject matter, taking us into every nook and corner of every constituency. It is almost a repetition of the procedure in respect of estimates. Is there a more embarrassing regulation than the one which allows an hon. member to speak for thirty-nine minutes and, after an interruption which gives him an opportunity to take his seat, to rise again and keep on talking for another thirty-nine minutes, and so on? There should be a ten-minute limit; and hon. members should not have the right to speak twice on the same section of a bill. Since we are handed bills beforehand, this procedure would compel hon. members to examine them in advance, thus giving them an opportunity to prepare their questions, instead of waiting until they have taken their

The Address-Mr. Lapalme
seats in the house and proceed to ask irrelevant questions, as so often happens, on account of lack of preparation.
Since I have been referring to the house sitting as a committee of the whole, perhaps I might deal with the permanent or standing committees, and their reports which are subsequently brought before the house. We all know why those committees were created. They are supposed to speed up parliamentary procedure and somehow to clear the ground, thereby performing a task which otherwise would have to be done by the house itself.
Why should we have the right to begin anew in the house a discussion which already has lasted for days or even weeks in a committee. We all recall in 1945 the debate over certain international agreements, which threatened to start afresh in the house, despite the weeks of argument which had taken place in the committee set up to study those agreements. Had it not been for the lightning move of Little Chicago that debate would have gone on and on, although each member in the committee had been granted an opportunity of exhausting his views. I believe that after the usual steps have been taken the report of a committee should be either carried or rejected by the house, without debate. At the most, hon. members might be entitled to explain in a few words their approval or disapproval.
However, the greatest waste of time occurs when technical questions are poured upon the house. This is all the more complicated for hon. members, because these questions are brought down unexpectedly, usually when the attendance is small. Furthermore, on most of those occasions the debate develops into private conversations. Mr. Speaker hands down his ruling, and an appeal is made to the house. The bells ring; hon. members hurry back to their seats and ask what is going on. Often those who are on the battlefield are unable to explain what has happened. A vote is taken-and we all know how much time is taken in the procedure of recording a vote. Three or four votes result in wasting a whole afternoon of the time of parliament. I recall arriving in Ottawa at about six o'clock in the evening and inquiring from a colleague what progress had been accomplished during the day. "Today", he said, "we voted." I learned that three or four votes had been taken on technicalities. Did the country gain any-tning that day from the work of its representatives?
Respecting these purely technical controversies do you not believe that the ruling of the Speaker should not be debatable or questioned? When housing, wheat, social
security and the reconstruction of the country are at stake, can we not pass constructive laws with celerity instead of taking pleasure, if it can be called a pleasure, in voting upon questions which are completely irrelevant to the welfare of the country? I am not mincing words when I say that for my part such performances are unworthy of parliament.
I will agree that the foregoing suggestions may seem drastic. Some of these I did not discover myself and I admit that others could be improved, but on the whole I think they are worth considering if we really wish to serve with deeds and not only with words. Words! Shakespeare must have had us in mind when he put these words in the mouth of his hero, "Words, words, words."
This brings me back to the present debate and to similar debates such as that on the budget. In these true parliamentary discussions the oldest tradition entitles a member to speak at large about everything and nothing. There are no restrictions concerning the subject matter. I have suggested already that the time limit on speeches should be reduced from forty to twenty or thirty minutes. I will suggest another restriction, an important cue:	the house should limit the duration of
a debate. After the party leaders have had an opportunity of speaking as long as they wish the house should then decide that members as a whole will be entitled to a limited number of hours of debate. For instance, the budget debate could be limited to twenty or thirty hours, after which the Speaker on his own would put the question to the house. The total duration of other debates should not exceed ten or twenty hours. With a twenty-minute limit on speeches, a debate of thirty hours would mean a total of ninety speeches, which surely is sufficient to clarify any situation.

I say "especially by the government" because, as I stated at the outset, my remarks of today w-ere inspired to me by a member of the cabinet. Some may think that I am now the unofficial spokesman of a government too closely pressed by the opposition, ivho would like to muzzle those of opposite views. Let there be no qualms about this. I have neither directly nor indirectly received instructions to speak as I did and, moreover, my suggestions would apply with equal force to the members of my own party. But this is what I mean by saying that my remarks were
The Address-Mr. Lapalme

inspired by a member of the cabinet. When complaining in New York about the time taken for the drafting of the principles which are to guide the world of tomorrow, the Right Hon. the Minister for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) said certain things which brought to my mind my present observations. It surely never dawned on him that one of us would one day repeat his argument in this house. Nevertheless, it is his appeal to the united nations that prompted me to express here certain ideas which I had in mind ever since my first coming to Ottawa. Today I express them in all sincerity.
Having remained silent during two sessions, except on one occasion, I feel that I have a right to criticize the rules of the house regarding the number and length of speeches and debates. Like other hon. members, I could have made several speeches during each session, although I might not have spoken as well as they did. A glance at the roster of speakers prompted me to back up each time I intended making a speech, because I found the list too long and felt that among so many others, the effect of my speech would be lost. I may have thus contributed in hastening the business of the house, but I certainly did not do myself any good with my electors. However, if the rules remain as they are and we are compelled to work under the same conditions, I cannot promise to remain silent.
With regard to imposing a time-limit on speeches and debates, I must add that the list I have just given is in no way exhaustive. Many other matters would require attention. For instance, would it not be possible to put directly on record the speeches of sympathy or congratulations which take up the time of the house every now and then? Would it not be possible to refer the estimates to several committees simultaneously, thus shortening the time required for their consideration? I omit several other things which it would take too long to mention, because I would go on indefinitely when I am asking that speeches be shortened.
(Text):
It is interesting to watch the evolution of certain institutions which finally outdistance others that remain dead set in their conservatism. For instance, as a lawyer I have noticed that law is evolving more rapidly than procedure. For that reason Quebec is contemplating a revision of its civil procedure. The vehicle of law or legislation is procedure. In the physical world transport vehicles are endeavouring to outspeed each other. Speed

will never be great enough for travellers as well as for goods. Automobiles, aeroplanes, railways and liners have become the ultrafast vehicles of our civilization, and these will soon be transformed by the fission of the atom. Meanwhile parliament with the present vehicle of its legislation remains bogged down in the horse and buggy era.
I do not want to underrate the role played by this federal parliament. I am wTell aware that we are a deliberative assembly and the Canadian parliament is no worse than any other. Were I to compare federal and provincial debates I would not hesitate to say that the former are on a higher level. I do not underrate the role of this deliberative assembly, but I consider that deeds are more important than deliberations and that we should not attempt by means of deliberations to increase our prestige with the people.
If we wish to carry out the suggestions I have just put forward we have all the necessary means at our disposal. One of the permanent committees of this house which very seldom meets could be entrusted with the task of revising our rules, or a special committee could be formed for this purpose. I do not think I am mistaken when I say that the country would be pleased if its representatives would speed up parliamentary procedure and thus pass more quickly from words to deeds. At the present time parliamentarians do not enjoy such a good reputation. Is that not due to a great extent to their verbiage? It is high time that we lost this reputation.
If some consider that my remarks are a criticism of our parliamentary system they are mistaken. I am not criticizing our parliamentary system; I am criticizing only one of its methods. On the other hand, I want this to be a constructive piece of criticism. Those who have listened to me with great patience will realize that whenever I found fault with anything I offered a practical suggestion in its stead.
The house has the right to keep on with the same routine which is interfering with its work, but it also has the power to improve its methods. At each session improvements are effected in this building, but nothing is done toward changing the methods which should prevail within its precincts. I hope that the welfare of the Canadian people will be stronger than the old traditions and that some day parliament will be in a position to respond almost immediately to the request of the people.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

The Address-Mr. Murphy

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a back-bencher I wish to add my congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the address. The opening of this session will be remembered in the years ahead, not because the speech from the throne was the first delivered by the present governor general nor because we did not receive the summons in the usual manner. What impressed me, as I believe it impressed most members present on that day, was the incident which we find recorded on page 2 of Hansard when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) rose and begged leave to move, seconded by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent), a motion concerning a man whom we may now simply call Fred Rose. I will not read the motion, but after it was made by the Prime Minister, the Prime Minister added these words:
This resolution speaks for itself. I have nothing to add.
Then Hansard adds:

Motion agreed to.
And then deadly silence. Never within my memory has silence registered such contempt. I have no hesitation in saying that there is no room in Canada for those who would destroy Canada. There is no room in our legislative halls for anyone who prefers the communistic system to our Canadian system. Those who do not believe in the way of life which has made us the nation we are today should not be permitted to occupy positions of trust or of power in any part of our government, dominion, provincial or municipal. They should, they must be removed, and one was. Liberty, freedom of speech, of assembly and of press does not and must not be permitted to mean that the enemies of this country conspiring to overthrow by violence our governmental economies and social system shall have licence so to conspire under the protection of our constituion. Let the echo of their doctrines be heard only by themselves within the confines of prison cells.
On behalf of the vegetable and seed growers of Lambton county I wish to take this opportunity to express their appreciation of the order issued last fall requiring an import permit to import Dutch sets and shallots into this country. I do not know the amount involved in dollars and cents, but it was estimated, at $100,000 or better. Whatever it is, however, these growers are now assured of a Canadian market for their product at a fair price, whereas in former years their industry 83166-8
was in peril because in some years the United States, having a large surplus, exported its surplus products into Canada at a price much lower than our cost of production. I would be very ungrateful indeed if I did not express my personal thanks to the other members on both sides of the house representing adjoining or nearby ridings for their cooperation and interest in. this matter. To me it indicates what the members of the two old parties can do when working together for a common purpose.
I should like to make a running comment for a moment or two on my impressions of the last two or three days in the house. It was the first occasion on which I, and no doubt many other members here, saw new members introduced. I sat back here not knowing what was going to happen and was startled when I s£*w the Prime Minister and his right-hand man, jump up and walk to the door. Richard was not there to open the door; nevertheless it was opened, and. I learned that these gentlemen were about to escort the new member up the aisle. I had heard rumours before, during and since the election, that the new man might be a Mackenzie King Liberal or just a Liberal or a Cardin Liberal. I was not sure, but at any rate they took him by the arm, one on either side, and as they came up the aisle he certainly could not get away if he tried, he was so rigidly held. He approached the table and the usual ceremony was performed. When I saw him approach your dais, Mr. Speaker, I wondered, after hearing the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) the other day, in speaking of and to you, if the new member might be taking on the duties of Speaker of the House of Commons.
After that, the leader of His Majesty's loyal opposition (Mr. Bracken), and two of his large supporters retired in the same manner and brought in one Conservative member after another. Of course we all know that after the weather clears in Halifax there may be another by-election there and our chief the leader of the opposition will have to give another command performance.
After our leader had introduced the new Conservative members, the Social Credit party brought forward their champion in the same way. To me it was quite impressive. The next day a number of hon. gentlemen came in wearing carnations. There is of course a day in the year when flowers are worn in honour of mothers but I did not think all these her., gentlemen had the same mother. I did think, however, these flowers represented something and as we had heard a great deal about a possible change in the leadership of the Liberal
The Address-Mr. Murphy

party I thought that perhaps hon. gentlemen were mourning the retirement of their political father.
Yesterday our leader made one of the finest speeches ever heard in this house. It contained so much meat that the Prime Minister could neither chew nor swallow it. In the course of his remarks, the Prime Minister of course championed the Liberal party, but somehow the speech delivered by my leader cut deep and the remarks of the Prime Minister were certainly directed at my leader. If the leader of the opposition had delivered a poor speech it would have received no attention from the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister did trip over the five-cent piece; a little later on when he was advising this audience that the leader of the opposition had been remiss in his responsibilities, that he had not a knowledge of the proceedings of the house, it appeared to everyone that the motion of want of confidence certainly irked somebody, and the Prime Minister proceeded to lecture this party on that motion. After a while our leader rose and informed the Prime Minister that he had a good precedent for the motion since it was exactly the same as one which the right hon. gentleman himself introduced a few years ago. That was quite a fall indeed.
What impressed me however was this. The Prime Minister eulogized his party, which he seemed to think enjoyed the confidence of the people, but apparently he forgot that in the last four by-elections the great Liberal party won only one, so that, instead of having the confidence of the majority of the Canadian people, it would appear to have only twenty-five per cent of that confidence.
After the Prime Minister got through, there was great applause during which the leader of the C.C.F. rose to speak. I do not know whether he did it purposely to share in the applause given the Prime Minister but he did not sit down. He stared at the galleries in appreciation of the applause which he thought apparently he was receiving, and after it was over, in view of the rumours we have heard about a change of leadership, it occurred to me that those who were applauding were not sure whether they were applauding the present Prime Minister and leader of the Liberal party or the future leader of that party.
Mr. Speaker, I intend for a few moments to deal with a matter in connection with housing. The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) this afternoon dealt with that in a general way more capably than I could ever do it. I am going to deal with the matter specifically,

having reference in particular to the county of Lambton and the city of Windsor, with particular reference to the homes built for veterans under the small holdings provision of the Veterans' Land Act. I may say that I did not get into this until just a few days ago, a little before the middle of January, when five of these young veterans came to my home and told me that they had had an ultimatum from Mr. G. H. Parkinson who represented the Department of Veterans Affairs at London. Some few days prior to that he had given these veterans an ultimatum that they had to buy the homes within a week, move out within a week, or they could stay in until the first of May and pay rent. Two of the veterans had signed up, and I am going to speak about that matter specifically in a few moments; but others had not and they just did not know what to do inasmuch as Mr. G. H. Parkinson

"H" for Hitler, I think-was to return in a few days; in fact, a day or so after they came to my home. I want it distinctly understood that these veterans were young lads who had spent several years in the service of their country-. They lacked business experience; they did not know values. They were desperate for homes, and homes were scarce. They were married, of course, some of them having families, and they did want homes of their own. After their predicament had been explained to me, I agreed that I would go the next day to see the homes and inspect them. The next day I did go with three capable home-builders, men of experience. I may say, too, that I had seen the plans of these homes, and they are splendid. They are ideal floor plans and the homes from their outside appearance are of a very fine type. To me they were classified as a y'oung soldier's dream; and there is no question at all about it, they appeared to be just that. Anyone driving by the homes would think they were well built. I hope this condition to which I am calling attention does not prevail in many parts of the country, and I understand that it does not.

The Address-Air. Murphy
We made a thorough inspection of these particular homes. In the meantime there had been a great deal of publicity about the homes in Windsor and about these particular homes in Sarnia township. The grievances apparently were justified because the Windsor Daily Star, the London Free Press and the Sarnia Observer had been referring to the construction of these particular homes. Everyone in this chamber knows that these particular papers are certainly outstanding journals of the day. The Ottawa correspondent for the Windsor Star is not the only one on that staff or in that organization who has received or deserved empire recognition. As far as the London Free Press is concerned, the chief editor of that paper was just recently appointed chancellor of the university of Western Ontario. The Sarnia paper had sent out their own special observers to see these homes in Sarnia township and had printed articles about them. I say that before I go into the conditions of this construction, because it is evident to everyone that these newspapers were justified in carrying on a campaign on behalf of the veterans in Sarnia township and Windsor.
I might say, too, that these homes are not large homes. They are small homes. I should like to give the house the size of them first. I have the size of only three of them here. In Sarnia township there are only eight homes built, of four different types, two of each type. One was 18 feet, 9 inches by 32 feet, one and a half storey with basement; and the second was 24 feet by 30 feet, one storey; and the third one I have here was 25 feet by 31 feet, 8 inches, one storey. When we went with the veterans themselves to these homes we noticed that the septic tanks were not working. I have seen it reported in the paper that was because it is a one-tank system. I disagree with that. A one-tank system is perfectly all right as long as you have sufficient weeping tile. But these homes had been occupied for only a short time, and the only conclusion that I or anyone else could come to was that there was not sufficient weeping tile for these septic tanks.
We went into the homes, and I am going to describe quickly some of the faults, in view of the demand that I expect to make a little later on this evening. In the first place, in one home the water had come up to within three inches of the top of the basement floor. They had put a sump-pump in. That indicated that the water level of that property had not been taken before it was purchased for the veterans. When the water was that high at 83166-8J
that time of the year, it is needless for me to say what the condition will be during the spring or rainy season.
Then they showed us a floor joist. Everyone knows what that is; it supports the floor. Believe it or not, here was one joist with about a foot cut out of it. It was not headed, as would be done by an ordinary builder. The only thing that held up the joist was the floor above it. That was an unpardonable and inexcusable mistake for any building contractor to make. There was no occasion for such sloppy work. Mind you, this was not the only house where this occurred. These floor joists were not supported by anything except the floor above, which held up the joists. In more than one house the main beam supporting the joists was cut, in one instance about one-third and the other by more than that, which is also unpardonable and ridiculous from a building point of view. Chimneys were poorly built, with used brick, and not straight. They had very poor mortar joints; you could run a wire three or four inches between the bricks, and if you held a match up to the chimney the draft would draw the flame into the chimney. There were no water taps in the basement. I am not complaining about that, because I do not know whether the plans even called for them, but there should have been some. I do not know if the plans called for laundry tubs; in any event they were not there, and the wives of these veterans had to take the water upstairs and downstairs to do their washing. If the plans did not call for laundry tubs, well and good; but in any event there should have been taps down there. There were no water heaters in all these homes, and only one or two were insulated at all. The others were insulated in a small way by the veterans themselves. Then there was no sub-floor under the bathtub; and, believe it or not, the sub-floor under the kitchen and the rest of the bathroom was only one-third complete, one board and skip two.
We went into one house which was not sold, a one and a half storey house, and there the plaster board was off the ceiling; otherwise we would not have noticed what had taken place. There, believe it or not, we saw that the subfloor on that upstairs portion was the same as under the kitchen and bathroom; just about one-third sub-floored. I did not measure it; it was so ridiculous that anyone on looking at it would say it was a terrible job to palm off on a veteran. I wonder where the inspectors were. These homes were supposed to be built under government inspectors, but they must have been either blind or fit subjects for an insane asylum to pass work like that for a
The Address-Mr. Murphy

soldier or anybody else. It was terrible construction. A moment ago I was going to say that one of the housewives complained about the kitchen floor being springy. The inspector replied, "Yes, it is springy; it is easier to walk on that way."
Before I forget I must tell you, Mr. Speaker, about this Mr. Parkinson, who had two contracts signed. He went into the unemployment office, where one of these young lads worked, and practically forced him into taking over one of these homes. His language and conduct were such that some of the rest of the staff had to ask him to desist; and that is how this young lad came to purchase the property. Of course the homes did not call for plaster. It was plaster board, and the joints were terrible, with the corner joints an inch or an inch and half apart. Already they have had repair men come in, and they had to put quarter rounds in the comers. The kitchen sinks were well named; they sink. And get this. We examined the kitchen hardware. You know the hardware they have on the doors of henhouses, or the doors of the houses behind the houses. They use strap-hinges; and they had strap-hinges three and a half inches long on kitchen cabinets. Henhouse hardware, I call it. All they had was porcelain sockets, though they were supposed to have electric light fixtures in the ceilings. The trim was rough and soiled; it had not been sand-papered before it was painted. There were two and a half inch nails, such as they use for sub-floors, driven into hardwood floors; then they tried to countersink them and split the floors. Water was coming in the windows. The insulation was incomplete. In one house they had left two bags of insulation above the ceiling; they had not even bothered to open them, and the veteran himself had to put it on. I do not know what the plans called for, but they had only 500-watt water heaters, and that was not sufficient. Not even the bond timbers or plates for these houses were bedded into cement. The electric wiring was defective. There was no shut-off in the heat registers.
I could go on for an hour and a half describing the defects in these homes. They were disgraceful. I cannot understand how government inspectors could approve such work.

I regret to say to this
house that my friends built these houses, and I feel very badly because I must stand up here and tell the house and the people of Canada of such home construction for veterans. But if I am to be entitled to be elected to represent my constituency, or any other hon. members are entitled to be elected, our duty to our country comes before our duty to our friends.
After inspecting the homes in Sarnia township. I sent a telegram to Mr. Murchison, director of the Veterans' Land Act. Mind you these homes in Windsor cannot be compared with homes in Sarnia township. The Windsor homes have a splendid location; there is not a finer spot for veterans in the Dominion of Canada. They have sixty of these homes built around a golf club, but I do tell hon. members that the prices are far too high.
To carry on with what I was about to say,
I explained to the boys in Windsor the situation we had in Sarnia township. It was disgraceful and revolting; and if the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) could have seen those houses for himself he would have settled the whole thing in five minutes.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: May I interrupt my hon. friend, not to interfere with his address at all but just to inform him that as soon as I was told about certain complaints in Windsor by my hon. friend the Minister of National Health and Welfare I immediately sent my deputy, the director of land settlement and a special technical adviser to Sarnia and Windsor.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I know you did, and it is unfortunate that they did not see the Sarnia houses. My complaints about those houses came after your men had been in Windsor. My wire to Mr. Murchison was as follows:
In view of ultimatum of 15th instant by Mr. G. H. Parkinson of your department at London, presumably reading the directive to you, I have to-day with competent home builders inspected eight VLA homes in Sarnia township. Your ultimatum gave these veterans three alternatives. 1, to sign contracts within a week; or 2, to vacate within a week; or, 3, to pay such rent as may be determined by your officials but to vacate May 1, 1947. Have advised veterans to request new purchase contracts at fair price.
Later I received a wire from the acting director of the Veterans' Land Act which suggested I was not familiar with the terms, but there was no misunderstanding by me. Again I wired Mr. Murchison to say that- I had inspected the Windsor homes and contended that the prices were too high. I could go on for a long time describing the way in which these homes were built, but my main complaint is in regard to the Sarnia townshiD

The Address-Mr. Murphy
homes. I repeat, the Windsor homes could be repaired without a great deal of labour, but I am sure the prices are far too high, and other builders have constructed similar homes for veterans in the same neighbourhood at much lower prices.
I notice that Mr. Parkinson was quoted on January 30 in the Sarnia Observer as follows:
A crew of men from the Ryan Construction Company arrived at Sarnia this week with a load of material and have already started the improvements.
Mr. Parkinson requested the veterans to complete purchase contracts for the houses at a meeting held two weeks ago. The veterans declined to sign until they had written assurance that certain repairs and refinements to the houses would be done. The director said he could not include this clause in the contract but assured them the work would be done well.
He said to-day he would personally supervise the work and would remain in Sarnia for the next few weeks. The Ryan firm will bear the entire cost and will work from a line of faults made up by an impartial contractor of Hamilton, Mr. Parkinson said. He commented on the price of the houses. He said, "I feel that the prices of these houses are not out of line at all. They were appraised by competent builders."
I challenge that statement immediately. There is no competent builder in the Dominion of Canada who would appraise those houses within twenty-five per cent to forty per cent of what the soldiers are being asked to pay for them. In that statement I am referring to Sarnia.
I notice that according to order in council P.C. 419/202 of January 17, 1947, veterans are now given permission to rent these homes, pending completion of the deals. Number 5 of the order states that the period for rental shall not be in excess of one year. I suggest to the government that under these conditions I do not believe one year is long enough. No matter how the houses are repaired, I do not think the Sarnia people will ever take them. They should be given an opportunity of renting these homes for at least two or three years, until they can build homes for themselves, to their own satisfaction.
I emphasized at the outset that the press had supported these veterans. And from the little I have said this evening I think it will be agreed that they were moderate and fair in the stand they took on behalf of these veterans. It is difficult for me to figure out why the job of building homes for veterans should be more of a problem than the making of weapons of destruction in the prosecuting of a war.
I am not the only one who is wondering if the taxpayers' money was well and wisely spent on these Veterans' Land Act projects.
Fair consideration must be given to the veteran. He is the producer of the future and will pay a large share of the tax bill.
The seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne stated that our prospects were bright. A cheery thought; but it is far from being a factual estimate of the national economy. If he is correct it is because the voters of Parkdale, Pontiac and Portage la Prairie indicated in a way the government understands that the practice of borrowing and spending money like water must come to an end.
Our wealth is in the youth of the nation, these veterans. They are the trustees of posterity. We know the veterans' place in history is secure. Surely we do not need a special bill of rights to assure them the right to economic security.	[DOT]
Through the golden fabric of our laws runs a golden thread preserving the rights of the individual. Therefore, in view of the excessive and outrageous prices asked by the government for these veterans' homes and in view of the manner of their construction, I respectfully ask that a royal commission be appointed to make a full inquiry.

speechtext: Right across Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Therefore on behalf of the taxpayer and the veterans who were fortunate enough to return and not have their blood crimson the bloody soil of Hitler's devastated Europe, I demand that a royal commission be appointed to inquire into all contracts for purchases of land acquired for small holdings under the Veterans' Land Act,- to inquire into all contracts for the building of homes for veterans under the Veterans' Land Act and contracts for the construction of roads, the installation of water mains and other costs involved in the purchase price of these homes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as is my practice, at the end of last session I returned to Winnipeg to report there to my constituents as to what had happened in parliament. In return they did me the honour of informing me as to what they thought should be brought up in parliament at this session. Therefore I am charged with the responsibility of presenting to this house, and more especially to the government, their desires in the matter.
One of the questions which is causing grievous alarm is the way in which the price ceiling has been punctured, if not exploded. Yesterday the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) during the course of his speech took some credit to himself for the main-
The Address-Mr. Stewart

tenance of the price ceiling. Obviously the right hon. gentleman is not a housewife. Obviously he does not go out to purchase the food he requires for himself. It is equallj' obvious he does not know many housewives in Canada. Otherwise he would have learned that the average housewife in the dominion does not believe the bureau of statistics when it states that the cost of living has risen only by some 27 per cent. Instead she believes that the cost of living, with wdiich she comes in contact every day, has risen by something closer to 40 per cent or even 50 per cent.
Of all the price increases the most notable and perhaps most scandalous is the increase in the cost of milk. The house will recall that last August a motion by the C. C. F. party was brought before the chamber asking the government to reconsider its decision to remove milk subsidies. The content of the speeches made in support of that motion was to the effect that the government should maintain these subsidies.
As the leader of our group, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) said, we have been told on many occasions by the Prime Minister that parliament would decide. Parliament decided in no mean way when it defeated the government in a vote on this issue, and virtually instructed the government to continue subsidies. As we have been told, despite his avowals the Prime Minister flouted the will of parliament. The result will be grave for many families.
We have been told by experts employed by the federal government that every child should have at least one quart of milk a day. For a family of five, let us say, in Winnipeg North, if each child were to receive its proper supply of milk the cost to the wage-earner would be at least ten per cent of his income, an amount which obviously is out of all reason when one considers the many other things which have to be bought. Therefore milk will not be purchased. Those who are going to suffer most by the government's policy are, once again, the children of Canada.
We have been told, and again by experts, that one of the finest all-round foods for children is milk. But because of the government's policy tho/e children are being denied the milk they need. I had hoped hon. members opposite had learned a lesson from the depression and the war which followed. Many of us must have read with amazement the statement of a cabinet minister informing us that almost half the young men of Canada who volunteered for active service were rejected from category A because they were physically unfit. I know of no more scathing

indictment of a government or of an economic system than to permit a condition to exist which allows almost half of our youth to grow up physically unfit. That is the situation. When we examine into the cause of this unfitness we find that most of it is due to malnutrition. When we pursue it further we find that most of that malnutrition is due to the lack of an adequate supply of milk.
I repeat that by carrying out this policy of refusing to subsidize milk the government is jeopardizing the health of the children of Canada. The workers in the cities do not ask that they be supplied with cheap milk at the expense of the farmer. They hope and expect to see the farmer get a fair and just price for what is produced on the farm. But they do say that this is a matter of health, something in which the dominion parliament should be vitally interested, and they are asking that these subsidies be reimposed.
There is another matter with which I should like to deal, a matter not affecting the youth of the nation but those at the other end of the age scale, those who are in receipt of old age pensions. The pension paid in Manitoba today is a miserable pittance averaging less than $25 a month. We know that that sum is not enough to live on. My own investigations have shown that many old age pensioners are paying in the neighbourhood of $12 to $18 a month in rent alone, leaving them an average of less than $10 a month on which to subsist. Not only that, our aged have to wait until they have reached the age of seventy years before any care is taken of them. It has been argued that they ought to have saved money during their lifetime to look after their old age, but when one considers the average wages paid in this country during the thirties and before that, one sees how impossible it was for any wage-earner to save at all. In the proposals of the Dominion of Canada made at the dominion-provincial conference, this statement appears:
A strong ease can be made for reducing the age limit to 65 in order to provide assistance at least for those in the age group of 65-69 who are actually in need.
That proposal was made by the government. If that was the government proposal, why has the government not implemented it? Why does the government not put that proposal into action? One other thing. There is an almost unanimous desire that the means test be abolished. I know the argument is made that if the means test were abolished many who were undeserving financially would receive pensions. I would sooner see the

The Address-Mr. Stewart
means test abolished and the undeserving get pensions than see the means test maintained and those who need a pension denied it.
Let me give two specific examples. A small delegation of superannuated employees of the Canadian National came to see me some weeks ago. They told me how they had been superannuated at the age of sixty-five years with pensions ranging from $20 to $25 a month. If they lived to the age of seventy years and were able to obtain an old age pension, that pension would be whittled down until they would be little better off. Considering it from the point of view of those pensioners of industry, it is essential that the means test be abolished.
There is another group for whom this house has some moral responsibility, the superannuated civil servants of Canada. They find themselves in the same predicament as the superannuated workers of the railroad. What is even worse, these superannuated civil servants have never received any increase in pension to counteract the obvious and undoubted increase in the cost of living during the years of war. I hope the government will realize its responsibility to the men and women who have faithfully and loyally served this country and give them the increase which they deserve. On all sides, then, there is agreement that the means test should be abolished.
As a result of a debate held last year on old age pensions initiated by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), the then Minister of National Health and Welfare placed a table upon Hansard and he said:
From sixty-five to sixty-nine, 69 per cent are employed. In other words, if you extended the non-means test plan down to the age of sixty you would be paying money to a large group of people who were gainfully employed.
What are the implications of that ministerial statement? Almost 70 per cent of our old people between the ages of sixty-five and sixty-nine years are working. Does he believe for one moment that a man of sixty-eight years willingly gets up at six or seven o'clock in the morning, goes to his daily toil and works through until six or seven o'clock at night for the sheer pleasure of working? Does he not know that by compelling people in that age range to work we are appreciably cutting down the number of days they will have to live? Does he think that those old people work for the sheer pleasure of working? They work for the reason given in the advertisements of the insurance companies. We have been told that 90 per cent of the people of this country who reach the age of sixty-five years are either destitute, living on charity or compelled to work in order that they may
live. Those old people are working because of necessity, and it is morally indefensible to compel old people to work like this. If we had recognized our obligations to them we would have pensioned them off long ago.
My constituents, and I imagine many of the people in other constituencies, are asking that the means test be abolished, that the age be lowered to sixty-five years and that the pension be increased appreciably at least to $50 a month.
There is one other matter of some concern to which I should like to refer. I find among the organized workers a general demand that there be a labour code all across Canada. The workers are asking for this because they realize that it will add appreciably to the unity of this nation about which we talk so much and do so little. I am not going to discuss this in detail now because I intend to wait until the proposed legislation of the government is before the house.
But this situation I must bring before this parliament even though it affects only a small handful of men. I do so because there is a vital principle at stake. The case of the employees of the Canadian Pacific who were on strike in Winnipeg in 1919 has been taken up by almost every union. In 1904 the Canadian Pacific Railway Company inaugurated a non-contributory pension plan. In wage negotiations after that time the railway unions were always reminded by the company that the contributions to the pension fund were in lieu of raises in wages. When the unions asked for raises they were told, "No; we are paying this extra money into the pension fund for you." Therefore the workers naturally felt that they had an equity in the fund.
What happened when the strike took place? The Canadian Pacific took the position that the strike constituted a break in service and no pension benefits earned prior to 1919 have been paid to C.P.R. employees who participated in the 1919 strike. Be it noted that the Canadian Pacific is the only organization which has discriminated so flagrantly against the workers involved in that strike. When the case of those who had been pensioned or who were still working and were not eligible for a pension was brought before the company, Mr. Coleman, the then vicepresident, stated in 1939:
We have kept in close touch with this matter over a considerable period of time, always encouraged by the hope that sufficient improvement might take place in the financial condition of the company as to enable us to realize a firm conviction which we have always held that, in such improved conditions at least, some relief might be forthcoming.
The Address-Mr. Stewart

The revenues of the company have improved appreciably during the last seven years and yet what do we find? The company still refuses to pay these men the pensions which are morally if not legally theirs. As a result of pressure brought to bear by the unions and by my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), that a royal commission be appointed to investigate this matter, the government eventually appointed an investigator. Mark you, this investigator was appointed at the request of the unions, and yet when the report was presented to the minister, did he convey its contents to the unions? No. The first thing he did was to give it to the railway company, then for six or seven months the railway company held that document and it was tabled only in the dying days of last session. It was not the railway company which asked for the report; it was the unions; but they did not see it for several months after the railway company had seen it.
Mr. Johnstone, the investigator, in that report, asked that a royal commission be set up. Yesterday the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) stated that no royal commission would be set up. I shall be gentle with the minister because he is not in the house, but I disagree completely with the position he takes if for no other reason than that if a royal commission were appointed to investigate the legitimate claims of these men it would report in their favour. Perhaps we cannot compel this railway colossus to pay these men what is their due, but at least we could bring, as a result of that report, a certain amount of moral pressure to bear on the railway, and if it did not carry out the terms of the report it would be subjected, and rightly so, to the moral obloquy of this nation.
There is another matter I wish to discuss, the question of immigration and the question of refugees. In the first speech I made in this house I said certain things about our immigration policy, and I have seen no reason at all for changing them. I said that some of the rules and regulations passed by the department were iniquitous, and that still holds. One of the regulations we have is this, we divide our citizens into preferred groups and nonpreferred groups such as Ukrainians and Poles, and those even lower than the non-preferred, naturally, as we would expect, the Jewish people. I should like the house to bear that in mind while I diverge a little.
I have a bone to pick with the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen), including Indian affairs, immigration and other matters. Recently, only last month, the minister was

in Winnipeg attending a Liberal convention and according to a report in the Winnipeg Free Press-I admit that these reports are not always correct-this is what he said:
Mr. Glen, who spoke at the Monday afternoon session, said changes in Canadian immigration policy are in the making-
I hope so.
-and he hoped to be able to announce changes in the regulations shortly.
I hope that is true. Then the report goes on, in direct quotation marks, to quote Mr. Glen:
"We have already done more than any other country so far in assuming the responsibility of getting refugees from Europe," the minister declared.
Quite a number of people came to see me about that statement and I said, "If the minister is correctly reported the statement is a colossal fabrication; there is no truth in it". To prove my point I read to them certain excerpts from Hansard in the first session of this house, where at page 3536 I asked:
How many refugees have been admitted to Canada since January 1, 1940?
The reply of the minister was:
There is no record of those who might be called refugees. I regret that I cannot give the information.
The minister could not give the information to the house then; he did not know. But in Winnipeg he suddenly found that the information was available, and if he was correctly reported he was either deceiving this house or deceiving the people who read that report in the newspaper.
To go further, on last year's estimates, at page 5495 of Hansard, in effect the minister said: No one will say that Canada's contribution in the matter of refugees is a very large one. That is right. It is a shamefully small and inadequate one and even yet we have no policy with respect to refugees. The United Kingdom, overburdened as she is, has taken in 200,000 refugees in the years of war; Australia is taking in 70,000 a year. The United States may not have played its full part but at least it has been much more generous, in ratio, than we have been in this country.
I think this house knows as well as I do that there is still unparalleled misery in Europe, a misery that is almost unbearable. This house must know as I do, if it has a Christian conscience, there are thousands of people in Europe who are only too willing to start life in a new country, but they have no place to go to in this world of ours. I do not ask that those who are brought to Canada be nazi collaborators because we want nothing to do with them. I do not want to see brought to

The Address-Mr. Stewart
this country those who aided nanism and fascism in any way whatsoever. But I point this out to the minister, and surely he must know it, that already these people in camps have been carefully screened and the collaborators and fascist sympathizers removed. He must know, too, if he is on the job that not only have these people been screened but they have been classified as to skills and aptitudes and we know exactly how many of them can do a particular job. We know that thousands of them are skilled in arts and crafts and trades of all sorts. This government, and rightly so, wants to take its place at the peace table as an equal with other nations. I agree with that. But if we are to take our place as an equal we must accept the responsibility that goes with equality and we must give succour and haven to many of these people in our own country. Here is a case where Canada can give great moral leadership to the world. Here is a case where Canada can give to the hopeless some hope which will encourage them to live. The information I got today from a man who has just returned from these camps is that in preparation for the expiry of UNRRA at the end of June, already there are groups of people who have signed suicide pacts. We are playing with the lives of people, and there is no time for that sort of
play-
What has been our policy? Let us examine it, and the best way I can do so is to give the house some examples from my own knowledge.
A year and a half ago a Winnipeg girl, Freda Yurman, came to see me. She had come to this country form Poland in 1939, and in her little Polish village her relatives and her fiance lived. War broke out. That girl's relatives were exterminated. Her fiance joined the Polish armed forces. His relatives were murdered too by the nazi hordes. The village was wiped out, Poles and Jews alike. This young man was captured by the Germans and taken to a camp where he was beaten and cruelly maltreated. Then he was put on a death train with others to be taken to another place where these people would be gassed and then cremated. He decided to fight for it, and with several others he made a break from the death train. He alone escaped. The rest were shot down like so many dogs. After God knows what vicissitudes and trials he made his way across Europe and eventually landed in Palestine, and to this girl's great joy she learned from him that he was safe. Remember, these two people mean everything in the world to each other; they have nobody left. I tried to have them reunited. I wrote the minister giving him the facts and asking
if he could not bring this man to Canada. What was his answer? In part he said: The first difficulty is that Rubin Thau is inadmissible to Canada under the regulations and it would require special action by order in council to waive existing requirements of the law.
What was this man's crime? He was a Jew% and therefore before he could be brought to this country we had to pass a special order in council to rescue him. Apparently it was beyond the power of the ministry; we had to pass an order in council, and the ministry was not prepared to do this. Yet, when the time comes, the ministry can move with great speed by order in council to filch from the people of Canada their freedom.
Not only was this man not admitted but, according to the documents tabled by the minister yesterday, a known criminal who was not born in this country was allowed to come to Canada by special permit issued by the minister. We will take criminals, apparently, but not those who need our help.
I pursued the matter farther. The minister told me, and rightly so, that obviously our troops had to have priority-our troops and their dependents. No one will cavil at that statement; we agree with it. The minister did not know what the state of this man's health was and I got in touch with Thau. He was medically examined by the health officer at Tel-Aviv and I gave the minister a copy of the certificate and assured him that I could obtain transportation for this Jewish boy by air.
What was the minister's answer? Let me read first what I wrote:
Surely the entry of this man into Canada will establish no precedent. On the other hand, it might do something to bring comfort and happiness to two people whose lives have been a history of persecution and whose future is in your hands.
What answer did I receive? It was indeed a brief answer:
There is really nothing I can add to what has already been said.
We could not pass an order in council to bring happiness to two people, but, as I say, this government can pass orders in council quickly enough to take our liberties from us and to steal our property from us, as was done in this country, and at times to abrogate the most cherished concepts of British justice. So much for that particular case.
If we are to take into this country refugees, on what basis are we to do it? On the only decent basis, that all people coming into this country shall have equal rights, not still on
The Address-Mr. Stewart

the wretched discriminatory basis which is contained in the regulations of the immigration branch, that basis which tells us, for instance, that Ukrainian people are inferior, according to the government's ideas; that Polish people are inferior. Many members of this house must know what a contribution these people have made to this country.
These early Ukrainian settlers came to this land not knowing the language, their only possessions strapped on their backs, and they were dumped unceremoniously by the railway companies on the most barren and infertile soil of western Canada, far from civilization and from medical aid, dumped on land where there were no buildings and none of the amenities of life. Yet it was there that they started to build, to erect and to create. They built mud cabins in which they had mud ovens which were used for heating the cabins as well as for cooking purposes. They were persevering. thrifty, diligent; they fenced and ploughed their land, and as a result we see today good farms, excellent homes, good barns, perhaps roads that are not so good. The children of these early settlers, whom this government regards as inferior people, are occupying positions of distinction in every walk of life in this country. I need only point to my colleague and deskmate, the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny), whose contribution to the debates of the house has added to their lustre, and yet he is considered by this government, under its own regulations, to be a member of an inferior, non-preferred people.
In what way, Mr. Speaker, are those who come from the Ukraine inferior? Are they inferior in thrift? Are they inferior in loyalty? Are they inferior in honesty, courage or independence? Are they inferior in their devotion to democratic ideals? Are they in any way inferior in respect of the numbers who laid down their lives for Canada? Of course they are not. We accepted from them their sacrifices; we accepted from them their lives when it came to fighting the very doctrines that we persist in carrying on, and we insult them in death by perpetuating those doctrines.
Let me read a short statement by the Very Reverend Doctor W. Kushnir of the Ukrainian-Greek-Catholic church in Canada:
The last war taught us that there are no superior races and no inferior races, that the superior races might easily become the inferior races and vice versa, that we are all dependent upon each other for mutual protection, that the old shibboleths and signals are obsolete, that narrow nationalism must give way to a broader community of nations, in fact, a more genuine brotherhood of all the people of the world.
I would to heaven the government would heed that and act upon it.
[Mr. Stewart.}

speechtext:
The house will remember that a few weeks ago there was held in this city a ceremony of citizenship at which the Prime Minister was present and spoke, and at his elbow there was a little elderly woman of Polish descent from Winnipeg, Mrs. Mynarski. I had been at a ceremony in Winnipeg some weeks earlier where she was giv&i a posthumous award granted her son. He had died in the noblest way a human being can die, by giving his life for his comrade, and this award was granted fof his gallantry, the highest decoration which the empire can bestow, the Victoria Cross. That family is worthy of honour in this country, and yet it belongs to a class of people who are discriminated against as one of the inferior people, under these very same regulations. Why talk about our virtues of citizenship, or our ideals of citizenship when we have these regulations still used by one of our government departments?
The Polish people came to this country many years ago. They, too, went to the west. They built their settlements and churches. They ploughed the fields and tilled the land and made a garden out of what was almost a desert. They have taken their part in industry and commerce. They fought alongside other Canadians and died with other Canadians in the struggle against the same sort of doctrine against which I am fighting. The memorial to all these immigrants in western Canada may not be engraved on tablets; their memorial is in the fields of grain which wave in the prairie breeze, in the railways which span this country, in the bridges which cross its gorges, and its rivers and in the factories which they have helped to build and in which they labour. Yet we still regard them in these regulations as being a nonpreferred group of people.
There is still another group who do not come under this stigma, but we find them in the camps in Europe in large number. They are those of German descent from countries adjacent to and adjoining Germany. Most of them have fought fascism and nazism throughout all these years. Now they, too, are homeless. Now they, too, are destitute. We know the contribution which people of German descent have made to Canada. Then let us realize that these potential immigrants can make a similar contribution, and let us welcome them to this country. For the last twenty-five years, so far as immigration goes,
apart from rescuing refugees which I have been talking about, we have had no policy at all unless one calls a policy the purely negative attitude of exclusion based on the fears and terrors of depression days. Every minister of immigration has found ample excuses to make. In the last two years our present minister has had good excuses and valid ones. I do not quarrel with him for that. But surely in two years he should have had time to think of a policy for this country. We do not yet have one. I suggest to him that we should survey our resources and, having done so, should then permit carefully balanced immigration, supervised and adjusted where necessary until our immigrants are integrated into Canadian life. I do not ask for the open door, nor do I ask for mass immigration. We certainly do not want in this country another flood of cheap labour designed to break the labour market. What I ask for as a policy, and what I would agree with to a considerable extent, are the submissions made by both labour congresses. But above all, let me remind the minister again that any policy which brands an immigrant from the Ukraine or Poland- as non-preferred and which discriminates against him, or any policy which excludes Jews because of their religion, should be immediately rescinded in the name of democracy and in the name of decency.
