Mr. Speaker, I am in complete agreement with the sentiment which has already been expressed by several members of the house, that speeches be as short as possible. As a result I will guarantee that I shall not have to be cut off. In view of that promise, I propose to forgo all compliments and make my remarks as brief as I possibly can.
To start with, I should just like to say that in conversation with the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) after he had completed his speech, I was most shocked and amazed to learn that the houses he described to us are being sold to our veterans at prices of between $7,000 and $8,000.

The Address-Mr. Harkness
The first thing I should like to say something about is the oil industry. I am glad the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is not in his seat tonight because I think he is a little tired of hearing me talk on this subject. However, an encouraging amount of development work went on during 1946. In Alberta 187 wells were drilled, including one particularly good well in Turner Valley, which served not only to extend the area of that field but also its life. In the Lloydminster field, which straddles the Saskatchewan-Alberta boundary, fifty-one wells were put down, of which some forty were oil producers, and a large drilling programme is in progress at that field from which we hope eventually quite a considerable amount of oil will be recovered. Had the government adopted the suggestions I made during the budget debate last year, the amount of drilling going on would have been considerably greater, and I should like to urge now that the tax deductions and depletion allowances advocated at that time be included in this year's budget proposals in order to encourage the discovery of oil which we need so badly in this country.
I should like to draw the attention of the Minister of Finance to two other matters whilst the budget is in course of preparation. A large amount of the low-grade crude oil produced in the plains area of Alberta comes from the wells mixed with water and sand. An apparatus known as a heater treater is used to remove these impurities from the oil before it is shipped to the refineries, and the use of this niece of equipment is essential to enable oil to be shipped in winter time, and to permit the companies to operate profitably at almost any time. The oil men have requested that this most essential equipment be allowed to enter the country free of duty and sales tax, and I trust the minister will bring forward a tariff amendment making this provision.
The other matter is the entry into Canada free of sales tax of iron or steel casing; in other words, pipe for oil and gas wells. This pipe is so admitted at the present time under the War Measures Act, but with the termination of the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act this concession will end, and it is strongly urged that its continuation be provided for by an amendment to the regular tariff schedules. The continuation of this concession is more necessary now than it was in years past because United States prices for pipe and the freight on that pipe have increased. All other drilling costs have also gone up, including wages; and, as a result, anything that can be done to lessen drilling costs will help materially to bring about increased production.
I should like to bring one other question to the attention of the budget makers. I refer to the eight per cent tax on all supplies to domestic consumers of utilities corporations. This eight per cent tax of course includes natural gas used for heating purposes, and the result has been that those of us who use natural gas to heat our homes have been discriminated against as compared with people who use wood, coal, oil and so on. This tax was a war measure, and it may be that the government does not intend to reenact it. If such is not the case, however; if the government are going to continue to impose this eight per cent tax I would ask that natural gas used for heating purposes be not included. I see no reason why users of natural gas should have an extra eight per cent slapped on them for the heating of their houses, as compared with anybody else.
The next matter on which I should like to touch is the application of the railways for a flat thirty per cent increase in freight rates. This, I believe, is opposed by everyone in western Canada, where the general feeling is that, no matter what may be the decision of the transport commission on the application, no increases should be permitted by the government until the whole freight rate structure has been reviewed and a system of rates introduced which would remove the unfair discriminations which exist at the present time. Particularly the situation should be ended under which goods of all kinds shipped from eastern Canada to the Pacific coast pay a smaller freight rate than the same goods shipped to points in Alberta.
As yet I have not had time to read the voluminous report of the royal commission on coal. I have read the recommendations of the commissioners, however, and I must say I am disappointed that the majority report essentially recommends that things be left as they were before the war. I was particularly disappointed to find that the commissioners could not see any possibility of a large-scale extension of the market for western coal in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. I should like to make it clear that I am not taking issue with the commissioners; I am merely disappointed that this should have been their finding. The minority report of Mr. Angus Morrison did suggest that there was a potential market in northwestern Ontario for a certain amount of western coal which could be developed at slight extra expense, and I trust that his recommendations in that regard will be implemented.
I should like now to say something about defence matters. Apparently the defence pro-
The Address-Mr. Harkness

gramme presented to us during the last two sessions of parliament has been materially altered. On January 16 it was announced that the over-all strength of the permanent defence force would be cut from 51.000 to 38,000 men. At that time the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) was reported in the press as stating that there would be no definite decision as to what kind of defence force the dominion would have. In other words, in 1947 we are to have a period of marking time as far as defence matters are concerned. Reserve forces will be left more or less in a state of suspended animation, with no real effort made to "recruit them to strength, and with their programme of training greatlj- emasculated. Apparently this is being done in the interests of economy, but it looks very much like a return to the situation which prevailed between the two wars, when defence was very badly starved and almost completely neglected; and I trust that it is not the first sign of a return to those conditions. During the past two sessions members of this party repeatedly asked the government to state its defence policy, but always without success. The recent statements confirm our fears as to the situation; that is, that there was no defence policy, and that, as a result, the government has had nothing to state. I think it is now clear from what has been said by the minister that all the plans so enthusiastically expounded by the ministers concerned during the past two sessions were not based on any sound foundation of general policy, and, as a result, amounted to nothing, and have now in effect been scrapped. Possibly even the money spent on them so far has been more or less wasted.
With the general concept of economy in national defence matters I am thoroughly in agreement. However, I question very much whether the government's efforts toward economy have been launched in the right direction. I wonder if the large and expensive collection of officers maintained last year in Washington has been materially reduced, or is it still functioning full blast there while at the same time the numbers in our cadet forces have been cut in two? Further, we find reserve units with an authorized strength of 700 or 800 men which are authorized at the present time to send only twenty men to a summer camp for training this year. That is a question I would ask the minister to answer at some time in this session.
There is one instance of waste, coupled with reduced efficiency, which I should like parliament to bring to the attention of the house. It is the amalgamation of military district No. 13 headquarters with headquarters western

command, and the projected movement of the personnel of the former military district headquarters from Calgary to Edmonton.
When the announcement was made that the eleven district headquarters in Canada were to be absorbed in five commands I was hopeful that the movement would result in the elimination of the duplication of staffs, and a considerable saving in man-power and money. Upon looking into the matter, however, I was astonished to be told that the only saving in all Canada brought about by the change would be the elimination of five staff officers. Surely that is not a great saving, in the light of all the ballyhoo which went on about the matter, and the high hopes held out.
Upon examination of the situation so far as military district No. 13 and western command are concerned, I was more than surprised to find it would result in greatly increased expenditures. This is an increase which I estimate will run to at least a half a million dollars in the next three to five years, and, if any building programme is undertaken, will run to very much more than that. All this, I believe further, is accompanied by a decrease in efficiency.
Ever since it was formed, Calgary has been the headquarters of military district No. 13. The department has at that point a physical set-up for such headquarters as western command has now become. The placing of headquarters at Edmonton, however, will entail the purchase or construction at that point of buildings running into very large sums of money, in order properly to house and to look after the headquarters. There is no possibility of erecting those buildings at the present time, in view of the present state of housing in Canada. I understand the plan is to use temporary huts and things of that sort. But that is not going to prevent the expenditure of this money in the future, if the present plan goes forward.
So far as the immediate extra cost is concerned, the number of personnel to be moved from Calgary to Edmonton consists of 200 officers and men who, with their families, make up about 600 persons. My information is that the cost to the government of moving these people will be a minimum of $140,000, and will probably run to $200,000. Because of the acute housing situation in Edmonton the majority of the families will not be able to move, and will have to remain in Calgary for many months, and probably years. During all that time the men concerned will be entitled to draw what is described in army pay offices as separated family allowances. I

The Address-Mr. Harkness
estimate that these separated family allowances will run to more than $5,000 a month. This is an added and unwarranted expense which, as I say, will probably continue for years.
On the other hand, if the command headquarters which, I may say, has been at Edmonton for the past year, were moved from there to Calgary, the personnel involved would be only fifteen or sixteen. Most of these men's families are not living in Edmonton because they could not secure housing accommodation. Therefore the cost of establishing the whole command headquarters at Calgary, from the point of view of moving the people concerned, would be negligible.
Furthermore, of the twenty-one permanent force units in Alberta eighteen of them, including I believe all the large ones, are located in Calgary. I understand it is not proposed to move these units, particularly services such as ordnance depots and shops, army service corps, and the like, because the cost to service the large permanent force units which would be left in Calgary and the reserve force units which are mostly in the south, would be particularly prohibitive if these installations were moved to Edmonton. Therefore Calgary will continue to be the chief permanent force centre in Alberta, with command headquarters 200 miles away from it. I believe two-thirds of all the reserve force units of Alberta are south of Red Deer, which is exactly halfway between Calgary and Edmonton. Thus, the result of placing headquarters at Edmonton rather than at Calgary will mean a great increase in the amount of travel on the part of the entire staff.
In addition to transportation costs, each officer when in Calgary and away from headquarters draws $7 a day command pay. The total increased cost of having headquarters at Edmonton will thus, from that point of view, taking into consideration transportation and command pay, amount to several thousand dollars each month more than has been the situation heretofore. In addition to this, delays of all sorts in dealing with problems of both active and reserve force units will be considerable. As a result, there will be a lack of or a loss in efficiency.
The mayor of Calgary and the board of trade, along with the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) and myself, have protested against this move, and asked the reasons for it. All we have been able to get from the Minister of National Defence in reply is a letter which he addressed to me on January 7, in which he said, in part:
I wish to assure you that the decision to make the move in question was arrived at on practical, strategic and economic grounds.
That is a fine explanation!-much the same as my stating that Ottawa is a better place than Montreal in which to live, a statement which could provoke a considerable amount of argument from many hon. members. But the minister's reply is in the same class. It is not a reply; it is nothing.
In his reply to the board of trade the minister said this, in addition, and that is all we have been able to get out of him:
Last January command arrangements were organized under five senior commanders whose areas of responsibilities were widened to coincide with the strategic defence problems of Canada. It was now possible to take advantage of various economies apparent in the plan.
And later on he states:
Command headquarters was also in charge of administration of active and reserve force troops in Alberta.
It would be uneconomical to have the two headquarters operating separately. And the commander should not be separated from his staff, the letter went on.
And a little further on:
I hope that the citizens of Calgary generally will appreciate that this movement is dictated by reasons, firstly of sound military organization, secondly by the necessity of achieving full cooperation between the armed forces responsible for defence and lastly, from the standpoint of achieving every possible economy in the employment of men and money.
All those so-called reasons are in my opinion only statements. The minister has produced no proof to support them. As a matter of fact there has been no specific and valid reason for the move except the possible desirability of having the air force headquarters, which are situated at Edmonton, and the army head* quarters together. Apart from that, no valid reason has yet been put forward.
I think I have shown that the minister's statement in connection with economy is absolutely wrong. If my statements are not correct, the minister should produce proof. All that we in Calgary ask for is that the move be postponed until it is shown to be in the interests of economy and efficiency. The minister has stated that it is, but he has produced no proof. We submit that the exact opposite is the case.
I happen to know that an investigation into the cost of the move from Calgary to Edmonton as compared with having the command headquarters at Edmonton, as well as into the relative strategic advantages, was ordered after the move had been announced. I should like to know why that investigation was not undertaken before the move was ordered or
The Address-Mr. Harkness

before a decision was reached. But now that the investigation has been held, what are the findings? I am very much interested in knowing that, and I challenge the minister to lay them before the public and before parliament here. I am sure they will bear out in a large measure my contention that there will be greatly added costs without any corresponding advantages.
The only possible reason that can be advanced for this move is the desirability of having air and army headquarters together. It is a debatable point whether Edmonton possesses any strategic advantages. I believe it does not. In the event of invasion from the north by air or otherwise, the tactical headquarters command would immediately move north to the area of operations and the rear headquarters would move back to Calgary to be with the services with whom their chief job would lie. In the event of any fighting actually taking place, which is the only thing which would provide any strategic reasons, Edmonton would be deserted.
Until good reasons are produced to justify the move, there are only two conclusions to which I can come: first, that it was dictated by political reasons. It is a well known fact that Edmonton has strongly supported the Liberal cause for many years, while the reverse is true of Calgary. That may have had a determining effect upon this decision but I sincerely trust that has not been the case.
The second and only other conclusion I can come to is that the officials at national defence headquarters made a false appreciation of what the situation was without being fully informed of the facts. I think the fact that an investigation was held after the move was ordered is practically an admission of this. I am afraid that, once having made that false appreciation, they are stubbornly sticking to it; because of a fear of loss of prestige or something of that sort they will not admit their mistake.
In other words, I believe this thing was decided by a few officials here in Ottawa who brought out a map, looked at it and said, "Oh, yes, there is Edmonton right in the centre of the province." It may be in the centre of the province geographically, but it is certainly not the centre of population. The centre of population in the province is much farther south of Edmonton. These people do not realize that. They also do not realize that most of the permanent and reserve units are in the southern part of the province and that this move will cause a great increase in expense

without any added efficiency. In fact the reverse will be the case; there will be a decrease in efficiency.
In view of these facts, I call upon the Minister of National Defence either to justify fully the projected move or to cancel it in the interests of the economy which we on this side of the house certainly desire and which the government professes to desire.

Mr. Speaker, you will realize what my feelings are when, for the first time, I have the privilege of addressing the Canadian parliament. However, at the thought that our country's population is anxious to have a government at their service, I feel somewhat more at ease and, at the same time, deeply deceived by the slight hopes given our people in the speech from the throne.
This afternoon, a member of the C.C.F. party took to task a statement I gave the Ottawa newspapers concerning a strike which broke out and still persists at the Noranda mines, in my constituency. The stand taken by the Union of Electors in the strike at the Noranda mines is very clear cut; they approve the demands of the Noranda miners who seek security for themselves and their families. When they ask for a wage increase, we are with them; we urge the government to insist that the Noranda mines guarantee security to these miners. Mr. Speaker, when the miners' union asks for a deduction of union dues from salaries, we cannot support this system commonly called "check-off" and I shall tell you why.
We look forward to a free Canada and free Canadians. We want our people to be free; we desire their protection; we do not want them to be subjected to rigid laws. That is why the check-off must not fetter the freedom of the Noranda miners, no more than that of other Canadians. By opposing the checkoff, that is the deduction of union dues from the salary, we simply wish to protect the freedom of the miners, the freedom of the workers. If a worker or a miner wishes to give his support to, and become a member of a union, he is free to do so; he is at liberty to join whatever union he prefers. But there will be some to object that the check-off or deduction of dues from the salary at the Noranda mine is entirely optional and that no one is forced to accept it. I admit it is so at the present time; but the heads of the Noranda union boldly tell us, for example, that next year they will ask for compulsory

The Address-Mr. Caouette
contributions, thus forcing the Noranda miners to join the CIO union at Noranda. It is precisely against this compulsion which may come into force next year, that we are fighting with all our might. That is a dictatorial method whereby the citizen is deprived of his freedom. Under the pretext that the union must have freedom and security we are told that the check-off is essential. Mr. Speaker, what is important to us in our Union of Electors or our Social Credit movement, and what is important to every hon. member of this house, is the freedom of the citizen; it is the security of the citizen. If a union enjoys security while, on the other hand, its members have none, and are continually faced with poor living conditions, suffer from depression, and get only low salaries, there is in such a situation nothing particularly advantageous to workers, miners, farmers or others, for that matter.
We want in the first place security for the citizen. When the miners from Noranda, from my constituency, or elsewhere, can obtain a fair salary, they will enjoy security and as a result they will be able to guarantee their union's security, provided they can freely join it. without being forced into it. It should be clearly understood that whoever is compelled to join a union never becomes necessarily an active member but rather a subversive member of that organization; and, instead of working in the union's interests, he will work against it, after having -been compelled to join it. Never will he tolerate being directed against his will to a place where his freedom, which he considers sacred, would be violated.
It is obvious that the C.C.F. party wants to establish a petty system under which Canadians will no longer be allowed to move freely but will be constantly controlled and will not be able to do anything without the government's consent. Well, Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the Canadian people want neither socialism nor communism in Canada. They want security, freedom, a system respectful of order and individual freedom.

If true democracy means every man's freedom and security, let us see what obstacles stand in the way of its achievement in this country. I shall quote, Mr. Speaker, from an address by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the general election of 1935:
Once a nation has given up control of its money and its credit, it does not matter who makes the laws of the country. As soon as usury takes control, it will bring ruin to any nation. The Union of Electors comprises Liberals, Conservatives, and followers of every political shade and hue. We unite not around a party, nor around a group, nor even around a party leader but in order to secure the objectives and results which the electors wish from the government. The Union of Electors advocates progress and that is why it wants parliament to have representatives supported by the electorate and not by party funds. The Union of Electors sets forth a very plain and very definite programme; it supports a policy suitable to one and all. Why am I a follower of the Social Credit party? You do or will understand. I am quite at ease with the Social Credit group. I believe it is the only one which recognizes real freedom of the individual, which allows one of its members to hold opinions different from those of the leader and other members. I believe that the Union of Electors will show its mettle in the house and that in the near future we shall represent the entire Canadian electorate in parliament. The policy of the Union of Electors is clear and well-meaning towards everyone.
Before I go into the details of our programme, may I digress briefly. I was not elected to vrage an obstinate and stubborn struggle against so and so. I wish to assure all the hon. members of this house that we can honestly and sincerely cooperate with another party whenever the interests of the people of Canada as a whole, and not merely of a section of the country, are at stake.
The very first point which we advocate in our programme is that all annual incomes under $3,000 be tax free. That is a big claim and the electors support that part of our programme. No one in Canada opposes it. All over the country, electors favour income tax exemption for those who earn less than $3,000 a year. I am sure many electors have not forgotten that the members have voted themselves a tax-free increase of $2,000 per annum. Added to their previous indemnity,

it brings the tax-free total to $3,000. These people felt that if such doings were in order for our representatives, they were equally in order for the electors. I therefore submit that they were right. Such is (he first point on the Union of Electors' programme. If it applies to members of parliament, I believe it should also apply to our constituents who have elected us and pay our salary.
Secondly, we advocate an equitable old age pension plan; let such pensions be paid at a reasonable age, before death and not afterwards. An old age pension of $60 monthly payable at the age of sixty. We contend that every person should receive a $60 monthly pension upon reaching the age of 60, and without investigation. Such a pension would be more Christian and humanitarian. Instead of paying the investigators, let us give that money to the aged.
Thirdly, we advocate a $60 monthly pension payable to all cripples and invalids at the age of twenty-one. At present, no Canadian law provides for the security and freedom of cripples and invalids. They must rely on their parents. No law provides for them. Should the government enact a law granting a $60 monthly pension to cripples and invalids at the age of 21, it would comfort them and they could look forward with confidence to a happier life than at present, free from despair, fear and the thought that they must rely on the help of their parents, brothers, sisters and other relatives. They have enough of their infirmity without having to live in a hopeless condition for the rest of their lives. That is why we are asking a $60 monthly pension, payable to cripples at the age of twenty-one.
The last point, Mr. Speaker, is most important and most pleasant for the whole population; I mean the national dividend of $20 per month. This national dividend would be based on the difference between the total value of our production and the total amount of currency and credit in circulation in Canada. We would make up the difference, balance it with the corresponding purchasing power and distribute it to all citizens alike, even to the hon. members, as a dividend. It has been contended-some have even said so in Pontiac county-that a national dividend would be absurd. It is said that the people who have money are lazy, that they are all lazy. It is said that they will stop working, that they will refuse to work any longer and that idleness will forthwith become the greatest evil in Canada. During the election campaign in Pontiac, the constituency I now represent and which is

The Address-Mr. Caouette
fairly prosperous, there were people who wanted to win that constituency with all its wealth, but no one among them was afraid of becoming lazy with the money he would obtain. Money is all right for some, but not for the common people, who might become lazy if they had it. Must we say that we have become lazy because we get that money? No. Neither will the people become lazy. Money does not beget laziness. People who have money are tempted to put it to work. A lazy millionaire has never been seen in Canada, Mr. Speaker. No, never. We have never seen a man who had $50,000, for instance, or a million, who was not anxious to make another million. But when a man steadily does hard work without ever succeeding ia saving anything, he becomes discouraged and gives up his job.
Mr. Speaker, a strike is on at the present time at the Noranda mine, and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) has a hard task in finding a solution. He receives telegrams and petitions to settle the Noranda strike as soon as possible.
I know that it is a problem, but it would be very easy to tell the mine to pay the 16 cents an hour increase that is asked for, because they admit themselves that they can pay that 16 cents.
There is something else, related to what I said a moment ago about exempting from income tax all income below $3,000 a year. At the Noranda mine as elsewhere, in each one of the constituencies of the hon. members of this house, there are workers, miners and farmers, and that is especially true of the working class, who will miss hours and days of work on account of that tax. They tell you openly: "If I work on such and such a day, I am going to lose it in taxes; I don't want to work just for the sake of paying taxes". So the worker refuses to work. He is not too much to blame. Such heavy taxes hamper production and work, and that is why I suggest that during this session the house should adopt by unanimous consent an exemption from income tax for all incomes below $3,000, so that miners and workers may keep their wages.
We are told that God gave this commandment to mankind:	"In the sweat of thy face
shalt thou eat bread". But let us not allow the government to interpret this as meaning that the miner and the worker must thus earn their bread 500 times before having the right to eat it once.
We have also heard of Alberta and of the Social Credit government. In 1935, the Alberta government promised $25 per month
to the voters, but they never got it. It has
never been said, however, that the dominion was responsible for that. No, such things are better left unsaid. It has never been said that the laws of Alberta had not been approved, but disapproved. No, let it rather be said that Mr. Aberhart, then premier of Alberta, met with complete failure in that province.
Mr. Speaker, if Social Credit is doomed to failure, why does the federal government not allow the provincial authorities of Alberta to experiment with the theory of Social Credit, to put it into practice, to place a rope around their neck and erase forever from the face of Canada the very name and the doctrine of Social Credit? But Social Credit measures are not. allowed to be passed by the provinces. They are constantly being stopped from doing so. Why? Because the government is well aware that if Social Credit were to be applied in Alberta, it would soon spread throughout the rest of Canada. Then there would be no divided political parties but a government responsible to the people and unafraid to give the people their freedom.

Mr. Speaker, along with the other hon. members who have preceded me in this debate I wish to offer my sincere congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the address, who have discharged the tasks imposed upon them with such ability and distinction. I only wish either of these gentlemen could lend me his rich voice for at least the time I shall address the house on this occasion.
Despite appeals made and hopes expressed by the different speakers that this debate on the speech from the throne might be made as short as possible, at this early stage of the session I must crave the indulgence of the house to bring to its attention a problem which in my opinion is of paramount import-
The Address-Mr. Michaud

ance to a number of people in New Brunswick and the maritimes generally, and which cannot wait until the estimates of the Department of Agriculture are brought before the committee of supply. I have in mind the serious plight which faces the potato growers of New Brunswick; and for fear that occasion may not arise soon for the discussion of this matter of urgent public importance I avail myself of the very first opportunity to deal with it as best I can.
At the outset I wish to point out that I am not speaking of my own personal problem as a grower, since my crop has been disposed of quite satisfactorily on local markets. I speak for the vast majority of the farmers of my constituency who have no alternative but to sell their produce at a loss. The potato is by far the most important of our vegetables. It is fifth in importance among our field crops, coming after wheat, oats, barley, hay and clover. Its all-Canada value for 1944 was estimated at $70,000,000, as compared with $460,000,000 for wheat, $263,000,000 for oats, $129,000,000 for barley and $183,000,000 for hay and clover. Of the principal crops it has by far the largest yield per acre. The all-Canada average for 1943 was 153 bushels to the acre. The average yield for New Brunswick in 1943 was 289 bushels to the acre, which is more than eight and a half tons. Our average for 1946 must be at least 300 bushels to the acre; for the successful farmer it is in the vicinity of 400 bushels, with some going over 500. The average for Prince Edward Island is not quite so high as that for New Brunswick, but it is considerably higher than that of any other province.
It is not only from the point of view of yield that Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick hold an important position in the production of tubers. From the point of view of total production the four leading provinces rank as follows, and these figures show the average for the years 1942, 1943 and 1944:
Bushels
Quebec	 20,000,000
New Brunswick	 15,000,000
Ontario	 12,800,000
Prince Edward Island	 7,000,000
The per capita production is as follows:
Bushels
Prince Edward Island	 45
New Brunswick	 20
Quebec	 3-7
Ontario	 2
From these figures it would appear that Prince Edward Island and some sections of New Brunswick have developed a highly efficient technique in producing potatoes economically and on a large scale. It must

be remembered that their soil and climate are particularly suited to the growing of this kind of crop.
To produce economically and on a large scale entails, however, considerable expenditure. A good system of rotation must be established; expensive machinery must be purchased, and large frostproof warehouses must be erected. Such expenditures for the average farmer run into many thousands of dollars. The potato grower who has gone to such expense knows his job, to a science; but many of them may not know so much about other types of farming. For all these reasons, once a farmer is organized to grow potatoes efficiently and on a large scale, it is not fair to ask him to change to some other type of farming.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, our potato farmer is highly efficient. He knows his job, and he does it well. He knows what yield may be expected when climatic conditions are favourable. Unfortunately, however, like the wheat grower in the west, he has no control over such climatic conditions. For that reason the yield per acre varies considerably from year to year. Thus in 1943 and 1944 the total yield for New Brunswick was approximately 17,000.000 bushels, whereas it was only about 11,000.000 bushels in 1945, and in 1946 it must be close to 20,000.000 bushels, with only a very slight increase in acreage.
Unlike wheat farmers, however, potato growers have no means of carrying over surplus crop in a bountiful year to a year of crop failure, unless the tubers are dehydrated; and dehydration is neither- economical nor practical. It is true that a certain quantity can be turned into starch, or put to some other industrial uses. But this also is mot economical for Canadian grade one potatoes. Industrial processing can hardly take care of all our inferior grade tubers.
So far as the export market is concerned, we have been fortunate within the past three or four years in being able to export large quantities to the United States. This year, however, there is a huge crop across the line, and there is no possibility of selling table stock potatoes to our friends to the south. We have been and are still exporting large quantities to Central and South America. Those quantities are mostly for seed, and that market cannot by any means take care of our surplus production. Generally speaking, the bulk of our crop must be marketed in Canada, and for table purposes.
What happens, then, when there is a bumper crop, like the one we now have on our hands? In the first place, a great many farmers have not sufficient storage facilities for the whole

The Address-Mr. Michaud
of their crop. They expect to sell a certain portion of it in the fall. Most of them have to do so in order to meet the very heavy financial obligations incurred in the producing and harvesting of their crop. When, as in 1946, there is a heavy crop, most of the surplus must also be marketed in the fall.
One does not have to be a professor of economics to visualize the effect of these large quantities of tubers offered for sale at the same time. Under such conditions the law of supply and demand goes into full swing and works havoc. Prices slump, sometimes to a point far below cost of production. Once the market takes this trend, there is no way to bring prices up, unless new outlets are found for the excess product offered for sale.
At present farmers in New Brunswick are selling table stock potatoes at a loss, and they have been doing so ever since late varieties came on the market at the end of September. When this situation developed last fall representatives of the potato growers came to Ottawa to interview Mr. Taggart of the agricultural prices support board. I accompanied the delegation which included the minister of agriculture of New Brunswick, two ministers from the provincial government of Prince Edward Island, the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton, a member of the New Brunswick legislature, and prominent gentlemen from Quebec and Ontario.
Shortly after this interview an order in council was passed, and the Department of Agriculture issued a statement outlining two methods of assisting potato growers, as provided in the said order in council. The first provision is for a subsidy of fifty cents a barrel to be paid by the board for potatoes used in making starch. Since this industry cannot afford to pay more than $1.15 a barrel for potatoes, the subsidy brings the total price, paid to the farmer to $1.65 a barrel, which is quite satisfactory, considering that potatoes used in making starch are not graded, and contain a percentage of tubers which cannot be sold for table stock.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What about alcohol?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That is not economical. Unfortunately at the present time there is only one starch factory of importance in New Brunswick, and that is the factory of F. W. Pirie Company, Limited, at Grand, Falls. This plant does remarkably well, and buys huge quantities of potatoes from farmers in the surrounding district. The fact remains, however, that it can bring relief only to a relatively small area in the vicinity of Grand Falls, and at the most to only one or two of the parishes in my constituency.
The second provision contained in the order in council to relieve the farmers is a guarantee to take over any surplus potatoes not disposed of through other channels, by May I, 1947, at the rate of $1 per 75-pound bag, inspected and loaded on cars at point of shipping. Whether this policy of the government has had any stabilizing effect upon the market is hard to tell. It is quite possible that, without it, prices would be much lower than those now prevailing. The government is to be commended for these two measures designed to relieve the potato growers of the maritime provinces, because otherwise I fear the situation would be nothing short of catastrophic.
In spite of these very helpful measures, the fact remains that at the present time potatoes shipped outside New Brunswick for table purposes do not net the farmers more than fifty to fifty-five cents a bag, which is quite a bit below cost of production. If the agricultural prices support board were to commence buying at once at the price of $1 a bag, as promised, and re-sell to retailers, it would automatically cause dealers to pay the same prices. The farmers in northern New Brunswick take the view that the marketing of table potatoes could be improved considerably by such action of the board.
A very reliable gentleman from one of the largest potato producing communities in my constituency has just brought certain facts to my attention:
First, that potatoes are in short supply in Montreal and a high price is being charged for them. This fact is corroborated by a medical man well known to me.
Second, a young man from my constituency states that the restaurant in Montreal where he usually eats serves potatoes only three times a week.
Another elector of mine has had to send potatoes to his sister who is living in Montreal because she has been unable to procure them at the store where she deals. My correspondent concludes his letter with the suggestion that the government take over immediately the distribution and sale of table stock potatoes at a fair price to the farmer.
Some hon. members may ask why the farmers are selling potatoes at fifty and fifty-five cents a bag when they have the promise of $1, less incidental expenses which would net them approximately ninety cents a bag on May 1. The answer is simple. In the first place, the farmers need money now to meet their expenses. In the second place, this government buying is something altogether new and the farmers do not know just how it will
The Address-Mr. Michaud

work out. Finally, if they waited until after May 1 it would not leave enough time before seeding time to market the huge quantities of potatoes which are likely to be left in the warehouses on that day.
To my mind, the only acceptable solution is for the agricultural prices support board to start buying at once instead of waiting until May 1. Assuming that the government, through its prices support board, were to buy all the excess potatoes in the maritime provinces, how much would it cost the treasury of the country, taking into consideration the subsidy at. present paid on potatoes being processed into starch? It is safe to assume that the assistance rendered by the government, to the potato growers will run into a huge sum of money.
The next question that naturally comes to our mind is whether the country can afford to carry out this policy from year to year. The United States has spent considerable sums of money to subsidize its potato industry. In that country there is a guaranteed price of something like $2.20 a barrel. In older to give the house some idea of what is being done by our neighbours to the south, I should like to read from a dispatch from Washington, dated December 31 last, which reads:
United States agriculture department officials predicted to-day that millions of bushels of frozen and rotten potatoes will be dumped under government instructions during the next several weeks.
They will be part of the 1946 crop surplus of nearly 100,000,000 bushels. Officials estimated the government's final loss on the surplus will amount to around $80,000,000.
I am not going to read it all, but the article concludes by stating:
The total cost of the 1946 potato support programme is expected to be $100,000,000. Of this amount, the agriculture department will recover about $20,000,000 from those sold to distillers, starch plants, live stock feeders and foreign buyers.
I think it is quite safe to say that we could not think of adopting such a policy for Canada. We simply could not afford such extravagance. In my humble opinion another solution must be found, a natural solution, a normal and sound solution, a solution which would not cost the government too much.
At the present time there is a de jacto minimum guaranteed price for practically all farm products except potatoes. In most cases this de facto minimum price is the maximum price as well. We have a maximum price on potatoes which came into operation early in 1942 and which affected the 1941 and subsequent crops. Because of this maximum price
[Mr. Michaud.1
which I consider fair and reasonable, the farmers have not been able to make the large profits which they could have made from 1941 to 1946, and which would have compensated them for heavy losses suffered in years of depressed prices.
Incidentally, I think I should at this stage point out how the potato market behaved on the same Saint John river prior to 1941. Prices varied anywhere from nothing or next to nothing up to $3.50 a bushel. In certain years prices were very good and farmers made good profits. In other years prices were considerably below the cost of production and producers suffered heavy losses. It was somewhat like a poker game in which the stakes were very high and the losses quite frequent. As might well be expected, many farmers went broke at that kind of game. Only the most robust financially were able to stay in the game and wait until they could pick up a winning hand.
The tragic part of this huge gamble is that it was in years of good crops that the farmers fared worst; they made their money in years of poor or average yield. Can anyone imagine anything more paradoxical, more tragic and at the same time more ridiculous? When a kind providence bestows upon our farmers a bountiful crop it might be expected that in a well organized economy benefits would accrue to the farmers. That seems to be the case with other agricultural products. Unfortunately it has not been the case with potatoes. On the contrary, our farmers are almost invariably penalized when a crop turns out to be above the average. Under the present set-up it is not the farmer who toiled and took the risk who benefits from a good crop. The law of the jungle prevails, with the result that the consumers and the middleman reap the benefits which rightly belong to the producers.
All this does not seem to make sense. There must be a solution. There is one which is being offered by the farmers and which is not materially different from that applying to other farm products. I have discussed the proposed solution with a great many farmers from my constituency, and outside it as well. Practically all of them favour some sort of government intervention in order to stabilize prices. I now propose to submit to the house, and more particularly to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), the suggestions indicated and urge the minister to give them his usual sympathetic consideration and see that appropriate legislation is submitted to the house during the course of the present session, if our suggestions are deemed to be sound

The Address-Mr. Michaud
and capable of being implemented. The farmers with whom I discussed this alarming question of depressed prices are of opinion that we cannot hope to stabilize prices unless we have:
1.	Controlled acreage.
2.	Orderly marketing.
They are prepared to accept necessary restrictions to that effect and, that being the case, I fail to see why anyone else should be unwilling to fall in line.
First, we must have controlled acreage. At this point may I remark that there does not seem to be much wrong with our present acreage. The best proof of this is the fact that the Minister of Agriculture has recommended only a very slight decrease in acreage for 1947, less than one per cent, if my memory serves me aright. No; it is not our acreage which is responsible for our present predicament. With an average crop in 1946, potatoes would be selling at ceiling prices all over eastern Canada.
With a fair guaranteed price, however, there is great danger of farmers increasing their acreage to a point where it would constitute a national problem of overproduction. There is something really fascinating about growing potatoes. Like other kinds of farming, it can be carried on more economically when conducted on a large scale. Naturally, every farmer who has possibilities wishes to expand and, unless some sort of check is placed on him, he will keep on expanding. For this reason it is suggested that the present acreage be not increased and that every substantial producer who markets otherwise than locally be given a quota based on his average production of, let us say, the past three years. To the extent of his quota he would be given priority to sell at a price which would ensure fair returns, a price approximating the present ceiling price, or possibly slightly lower. Any amount of potatoes grown by a farmer in excess of his quota would be at his own risk. In years of poor crops and good export markets he would probably be able to dispose at a fair price of any excess crop over his quota. On the other hand1, in a bumper crop year, like 1946, his excess over his quota would simply have to be dumped.
In a speech of this scope, it is not possible to go into the details of the solution suggested, and to meet all possible objections to it. For this reason I must confine myself to advocating the broad principle of controlled acreage. The details and the machinery to increase or decrease acreage could be embodied in a bill establishing a potato marketing board.
The second step toward this stabilizing policy could be termed orderly marketing and would work out somewhat as follows. Every carload of potatoes shipped by rail would be handled by the board, and sold at the price set by the government. This price should be sufficient to ensure a fair return even in years of poor crops. I can see no reason why the present ceiling price could not be made the fixed price. The consumers have paid this price until September last and, to my knowledge, have not suffered or complained to any extent.
Under a well organized potato marketing [DOT] board, prices would increase gradually as the crop year advanced, somewhat in the manner that the present ceiling price has operated during the past two or three years. Every farmer would be permitted to market the same proportion of his crop as his neighbour, during the same month or marketing period. Under the present order in council governing the price of potatoes, the lowest price paid is for the months of September and October. It increases five cents on November 1, five cents on December 1, five cents on January 1, and so on until June. This increase is designed to cover shrinkage and the cost of storage.
As a result of such orderly marketing, every farmer would have the privilege of selling his crop gradually over the crop year, and in such a manner that at the end of any month, if he so desired, he would have sold the same proportion of his crop as any other farmer.
Under this project the farmer would be assured of selling all liis quota, as human consumption would not vary much from year to year. But, if it should happen that the whole quota assigned to farmers could not be used up for table purposes, it could be disposed of at the processing price, and probably without any cost to the government.
This solution appears quite easy and simple to the farmers with whom I discussed it. Nobody would lose by it except perhaps a few consumers who would be called upon to pay a fair price for their tubers.
Before I resume my seat, I wish to make it abundantly dear that the plan which I have outlined briefly need not take into consideration areas where there is no necessity for this governmental intervention. It would have nothing to do with local dealings not involving the moving of carload lots over rail. It is felt that if the large quantities of potatoes moved by rail were marketed as suggested, prices would adjust themselves automatically to proper levels in other localities. It is the huge bulk of potatoes grown in New Brunswick and Prince Edward

Island and moved in carload lots which glut the market and cause these wide fluctuations in prices which are so damaging to our potato growers.
Our farmers, by producing economically and on a large scale, are rendering a real service to eastern Canada in forcing the price of this commodity to its proper level. Without them, Ontario and Quebec would be paying a good deal more for this much sought vegetable. In so doing, our farmers are making a genuine contribution to the economic life of the nation, and for making this contribution I submit that they should be given the protection to which they are rightly entitled by way of stabilized fair prices.
They must not be abandoned any more to the caprices of climatic conditions and the harsh law of supply and demand. Something must be done to bring about a saner state of affairs. In their name I have offered a solution which I feel is workable. If another solution is more acceptable let us have it, and let us have it soon before our farmers get too deeply into debt. I must insist, however, that whatever floor price is arrived at, it should be such as to ensure adequate returns to this class of farmers who never went on strike even when they could not sell their product. They played the game during the war years by submitting to a ceiling price. They lost considerably on account of this ceiling price. Let us make sure that they do not lose any more through failure to give them a floor price, and a decent one.
